skills.description: Lumera-style single image to editable 3D scene — VLM-parsed object boxes and parametric lights, per-object meshes, HDR probe, .tscn assembly, refinement loop.
skills.summary: Lumera-style single image to editable 3D scene — VLM-parsed object boxes and parametric lights, per-object meshes, HDR probe, .tscn assembly, refinement loop.
useWhen: turn this concept art or screenshot into an editable 3D scene with separate objects and lights
block out a level from a single reference image
reconstruct a room from one photo as movable meshes and tunable lights, not a point cloud or splat
build a bounded agent loop that refines a generated scene against a reference image
skills.body:
# Single-Image → Editable Scene Reconstruction (Lumera-style) in Summer Engine

## Outcome

Turn one reference image into an **editable, engine-native scene** in Summer Engine: individual `MeshInstance3D` objects with transforms, countable parametric light nodes, and an HDR environment probe — not a fused point cloud, Gaussian splat, or baked texture. This adapts the Lumera pipeline (arXiv:2607.20889, Tsinghua AIRSUN lab), which was built on another engine, to Summer Engine.

**Caveat:** Lumera has no public code, and the paper lists engine-portable extraction as future work. This skill documents the architecture and the parts an agent can build in Summer Engine today (assembly, scene representation, refinement loop, evaluation), and flags the parts that require external model components (VLM box/light parsers, per-object mesh generator, HDR estimator).

## When to Use

- Bootstrapping a level/blockout from concept art or a screenshot, where artists need movable objects and re-tunable lights afterward.
- Producing 3D scene conditions for 3D-conditioned video generation (a use case the paper calls out).
- You specifically need **editable entities** (instances, lights, probes) rather than a render-able blob.

## When NOT to Use

- You only need a visual backdrop: a Gaussian-splat or depth-mesh bake is cheaper and looks as good or better.
- Large unbounded outdoor scenes: the paper reports ~17 m Chamfer-L2 drift outdoors — geometry is unreliable at that scale.
- Exact light counts/positions are critical: individual-light localization F1 is 0.209 at 0.5 m; intensity error is ~2.7× (log-MAE 0.431). Expect hand-tuning.

## Core Principle

Treat image-to-3D as **game-engine structured parsing**: engines already store exactly the entities downstream tools need — object components, transforms, cameras, materials, environment probes, and countable parametric lights. The pipeline therefore parses those entities directly instead of reconstructing geometry first and deriving entities later.

Lumera's stages (from paper abstract + appendices):

1. **Lumera-Box** — VLM parses object-level 3D boxes (position, size, yaw) from the image.
2. **Lumera-Light** — VLM parses parametric light tuples `(x, y, z, r, g, b, I)`.
3. **Per-object mesh reconstruction** — a mesh per parsed box.
4. **HDR environment estimation** — environment probe (IntrinsicHDR partially compensates for SkyLight/unseen near-camera lights).
5. **Bounded agentic refinement loop** — dual-agent (geometry stage, then light stage) edits + verifies against the reference image.
6. **Assembly** — emit an engine-native scene (`.tscn` in Summer Engine).

Dataset backing it: Lumera-2K, 2,513 game-engine projects → 3.73M components, 63M object instances, 102.6K parametric lights, 95.1K camera views.

## Scene / Node Shape (Summer Engine target)

The assembly stage should emit this node tree so output stays inspectable/editable:

```
ReconstructedScene (Node3D)
├── Camera3D                    # recovered viewpoint (intrinsics from parsing stage)
├── WorldEnvironment
│   └── Environment
│       └── Sky (HDR panorama from stage 4) + ambient light settings
├── Objects (Node3D)
│   └── MeshInstance3D × N      # one per parsed box; transform = box center/yaw
│       └── unique material per object (so meshes are replaceable/refinable)
└── Lights (Node3D)
    ├── OmniLight3D / SpotLight3D / DirectionalLight3D × M
    │     # position/rotation from (x,y,z); color from (r,g,b);
    │     # light_energy from I (mind log-scale calibration, see Tunables)
    └── (the sky-light equivalent is carried by WorldEnvironment)
```

Keep objects and lights as **separate siblings under named containers**. That separation is what makes the scene editable rather than just looking 3D.

## Implementation Steps

### 1. Define the intermediate scene schema

Before touching models, define the serializable tuple set the pipeline passes between stages (this is the engine-native contract):

```gdscript
# object record parsed by the box stage
class_name ParsedObject
var box_center: Vector3
var box_size: Vector3      # must be > 0; validate (paper strips non-positive sizes)
var yaw: float             # watch 0 vs ±π/2 symmetry for near-square objects
var label: String
var id: int                # unique; duplicates are a known model failure mode

# light record parsed by the light stage
class_name ParsedLight
var position: Vector3
var color: Color           # r,g,b
var intensity: float       # I, log-scale calibration needed (~2.7x error typical)
var kind: String           # point / spot / directional mapping
```

Add a **repair layer** on ingest: drop/fix invalid labels, non-positive sizes, duplicate IDs. The paper notes sanitized evaluation silently removed these, and recommends constrained decoding or a repair layer in the inference path.

### 2. Box + light parsing (external VLM components)

Lumera-Box/Lumera-Light are VLMs SFT'd on Lumera-2K; there is no public checkpoint. Options: use a hosted VLM prompted to emit the JSON tuples above, or fine-tune an open VLM on your own engine-exported scenes (`.tscn` scenes are text and easy to export; this is the "build Lumera-2K for your engine" step the paper identifies as missing for other engines).

### 3. Per-object mesh generation + HDR environment estimation

Also external model components in Lumera (per-object mesh reconstruction; IntrinsicHDR-style environment estimation). For a Summer Engine blockout you can substitute: box mesh (`BoxMesh` sized to the parsed box) per object and a generated/estimated panorama `Sky`. Swap in real reconstructed meshes later without changing the schema.

### 4. Assembly: write a `.tscn`

Deterministic GDScript/tool script: instantiate the node shape above from the repaired records. A `.tscn` is text, so generating it directly keeps the output diffable and versionable. Save with `PackedScene.pack()` / `ResourceSaver.save()` from an editor tool.

### 5. Bounded dual-agent refinement loop

The paper's Algorithm 1 (Appendix H.7), adapted:

- **Two stages in order:** geometry (objects/boxes), then lights. Switch the agent scope and prompt head per stage, but **inherit scene state `s` and conversation history `M`** across the switch — this avoids a cold start and lets the light-stage verifier refer to object identities already confirmed in the geometry stage.
- **Each round:** agent proposes an action `a_t` (move/resize/add/remove an entity) given the history, reference image, and current scene state; the executor applies it to the scene; a verifier renders the result and reports `r_t` against the reference image.
- **Sliding-window history:** keep only the system prompt + most recent `L` action/report pairs (`M_{t+1} = Tail_L(M_t ∪ {a_t, r_t})`, per VIGA). Skip records adjacent to rolled-back steps. This keeps 30+ rounds inside the VLM context window.
- **Bounded:** hard round limits `T_g` (geometry) and `T_l` (light), plus early termination when the verifier report triggers it. Never run unbounded — that is what keeps this agentic loop "bounded" and cheap.

### 6. Evaluation harness

Reproduce the paper's metrics on held-out scenes so improvements are measurable:

| Target | Metric |
|---|---|
| Boxes | 3D mAP, IoU-B, F-score (Lumera-Box reference: mAP 0.1141, IoU-B 0.2472, F 0.2762) |
| Lights (scene-level) | non-empty-scene recall (reference: 0.998) |
| Lights (per-light) | F1 @ 0.5 m (reference: 0.209 — weak; expect hand-tuning) |
| Matched lights | median position error (0.261 m), median ΔE2000 color error (4.59), intensity Pearson r (0.628), log-intensity MAE (0.431) |
| Geometry (scene) | Chamfer-L2 (outdoor reference ≈ 17 m — large unbounded scenes drift) |
| Relations | SRF / anchor recall (known weak point; WildDet3D beats Lumera-Box here) |

## Tunables

| Parameter | Meaning | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `T_g`, `T_l` | max refinement rounds per stage | paper keeps 30+ rounds total inside context; bound them |
| `L` | history window size (action/report pairs) | trade context use vs. verifier memory of confirmed objects |
| Light intensity calibration | map predicted `I` to `light_energy` | ~2.7× brightness error typical; log-scale loss recommended by authors |
| Yaw symmetry handling | treat 0 and ±π/2 as equivalent for near-square footprints | explicit paper limitation; add symmetry classes or snap checks |
| Supervision scope (if fine-tuning) | lights whose influence intersects the view frustum, not just visible sources | authors' recommended fix for missing SkyLight/carriers |

## Failure Modes & Gotchas

- **Merged/baked outputs defeat the point.** If assembly emits one combined mesh or a splat, you've built an image-to-3D renderer, not Lumera. Keep per-object nodes + parametric lights.
- **Invalid model outputs are common:** non-positive box sizes, duplicate IDs, ID fallbacks. Validate and repair before assembly; the paper's benchmark silently sanitized these.
- **Yaw ambiguity** on near-square objects (0 vs ±π/2 look identical) — single-token yaw serialization in prior work does not handle symmetry.
- **Relation structure is unsolved** (object-to-object spatial relations): anchor recall/SRF are Lumera's weakest scores. Don't promise correct relative layouts.
- **Per-light localization is weak** (F1 0.209 @ 0.5 m) while scene-level light *count* recall is strong (0.998). Frame the output as "right number of lights, roughly right places."
- **SkyLight / near-camera lights whose source is off-screen** are not supervised; the environment probe (IntrinsicHDR) only partially compensates.
- **Large outdoor scenes drift geometrically** (~17 m Chamfer-L2); consider joint camera+geometry calibration if you need metric outdoor consistency.
- **Engine conventions don't transfer for free.** The dataset's light conventions come from another engine; Summer Engine's light units and probes differ, so recalibrate intensity and validate the representation on Summer-native scenes.

## Verification

Not yet verified in Summer Engine. To validate an implementation:

1. Assemble a scene from a test image; confirm the `.tscn` contains separate, selectable `MeshInstance3D`s and light nodes (editability check).
2. Move/replace one mesh and re-tune one light in the editor without breaking the scene.
3. Run the evaluation harness (§6) against a held-out set of known scenes and compare to the reference numbers above.
4. Confirm the refinement loop terminates within `T_g`/`T_l` and the history window never exceeds the VLM context budget.

## Confidence

`extracted` — Architecture, metrics, refinement-loop design, and limitations are drawn directly from the arXiv paper (abstract, intro, appendices H.7–I as retrieved; middle method sections were truncated and are not documented here) and the author's announcement post. The Summer Engine node mapping and GDScript schema are adaptations, not from the sources; no public Lumera code exists to reference.

skills.name: make-content
skills.description: Make a finished, postable video of your game, cut per platform and saved for review.
skills.summary: Make a finished, postable video of your game, cut per platform and saved for review.
useWhen: a developer asks for content for their game: a TikTok, Reels or Shorts clip, an X video, a trailer cut or a devlog
a visible change just landed (a boss, a skin, a level, a rare drop) and a short clip of it would do well on social
a piece of content came back with a Change note on the team's Today view
skills.body:
# make-content: a finished piece of content for your game

The person wants their game seen, not a content job. Decide everything and hand back a finished piece they only have to approve. Never hand back a plan, a draft list or questions you can answer yourself.

## The method: copy one real video, beat for beat

You do not freestyle. Real creators already found what works: copy their format one to one, beat for beat, with this game in it. Every piece starts from ONE reference video: a post from `content.list_references` (its clip from `content.get_reference`), or a real creator's video the person sends you.

1. **Study the reference first**, before you capture anything:
   - a frame-exact cut list: `ffmpeg -i ref.mp4 -vf "select='gt(scene,0.3)',showinfo" -f null -` (each `pts_time` is a cut; check by eye, lower the threshold for soft cuts);
   - a transcript of any voice, with times;
   - the text of every beat: its wording pattern ("POV: you...", "Day 12 making..."), where it sits, its size, when it comes and goes;
   - the sound (where the beat drops, where the voice sits) and the total length.
2. **Write a beat map** in `work/beats.md`: one row per reference beat with start, end, what happens, the text, the voice line, and which of our shots fills it. Every beat gets a shot; no beat is added or dropped.
3. **Cut to the same timings** (each cut within 2 frames), the same text pattern in our words, the same voice structure (as many lines, the same rhythm, the same places) and the same length.
4. **Check side by side before saving:** the reference and your cut next to each other (ffmpeg `hstack`), cut by cut. A beat that is off, missing or extra is a rebuild.

Never invent a structure. If no reference fits, pick another moment, not your own structure. Copy the shape, never the material: no reference footage (a trend swap's swapped clip is the one exception), audio or caption text in the piece.

## Hard rules (break one and it does not ship)

1. **Highest quality always.** Never downscale or re-encode below the master to get past an upload limit; a 4K master goes up in 4K. Use a path that carries the full file.
2. **No AI labels.** Never say or show that anything was made with AI: not in captions, titles, descriptions, on screen or in a voice-over.
3. **No reference audio.** Never post the sound of the clip you followed. Use the game's own audio, a score made for this piece (`makers.game_score`), or a trending sound the person adds inside the app.
4. **No credits to inspirations.** Never write "inspired by", never tag or name the creator or the game a format came from.
5. **Vertical is reframed, never stretched.** Crop or zoom each shot onto its subject. Never squeeze, never letterbox, never a blurred copy behind the video.
6. **No static end card on TikTok, Reels or Shorts.** The last beat is action; the play line goes over it.

Also: real game footage only for gameplay (never generated gameplay or fake UI); never claim a feature that is not live; never name other games in public copy; fresh shots for every piece (never re-cut an old piece with new text); no labels, glows, shadows or overlays the kit did not ask for.

## 1. How to run it

1. **Run it in a background subagent.** The coding session never waits. The main agent says one line ("Cutting a TikTok of the new boss; the review link follows.") and goes back to work.
2. **Asked: make it. Noticed a visible change: offer once, in one line** ("Clip the new boss fight for TikTok?"). Never ask about format, length or caption: decide.
3. **Find the game.** `team.list` gives the `teamId`. `content.list_games` gives the `contentGameId` (`content.create_game` when it has none). Then read, in this order:
   - `content.get_kit`: characters with pictures, colours, fonts, style, voice, do and don't rules, the store slug, and the Learnings section. The kit wins over this skill.
   - `content.list_references`: what performs now and fits this game, best fit first, each with why it works and an idea for this game. Your reference comes from here.
   - `content.search_library`: the team's raw clips, pictures and earlier pieces.
   - `content.list_pieces`: the last pieces, so you do not repeat them.
4. **Feedback first, without being asked.** At session start and after every `content.save_piece`, call `content.list_pieces` with the game and status `changes_requested`. A piece with `needsWork: true` comes before anything new: `whatToChange` says what the team wants. Fix it on the same reference and beat map, then `content.update_piece` with status `in_review` and `expectedRevision`. Nobody should have to tell you twice.
5. **Work in `content/pieces/<slug>/`** in the project. Add `content/` to `.gitignore` before the first file. Keep `raw/`, `work/` and `final/` apart.
6. **Deliver finished:** one render per platform, a cover, captions per platform, then `content.save_piece` and one line with the `reviewUrl`. That is the whole reply.
7. **Keep watching.** While the session lives, read each piece you saved with `content.get_piece` every few minutes. When `needsWork` turns true, act on it at once and say in one line what you changed.

Reload this skill any time with `docs.read` (`skill/make-content`).

## 2. Pick the moment, then the reference

- **Start from the moment:** what changed or what is best in the game right now. A new boss, a rare drop, a clutch win, a funny physics bug, a new skin, a milestone.
- **Then ONE reference** whose `howGamesCanUseIt` fits that moment. Skip expired ones. Choose by the viewer hook (why a stranger stops scrolling), not by how it is made.
- **Vary:** never the same reference format twice in a row; each piece differs from the last 5 on at least 2 of format, hook, opening frame, sound, length. A numbered series keeps its format on purpose. Over a week, at least half the pieces are gameplay pieces.

## 3. Reference shapes by viewer hook

What each kind of reference looks like, to choose which one to copy. The reference's own beats win over these notes. Lengths are vertical short-form unless noted; each example is a real, measured post.

**Trend swap with a gameplay payoff.** Hook: the viral shape, your hero as the surprise. 7-15 s, the source's length. Swap your hero into the trending clip (`content.make_video` for a library reference, or `makers.bankai_swap` with the source video and a picture of your character): the one shape that keeps the source picture. End on the same hero doing the matching move in real gameplay. Example: a costume walk shot feet first in one 15 s take, the camera tilting up to the faces on the drop (54M views).

**The reveal (the pull).** Hook: a rarity is coming. 6-10 s, or up to 50 s as a ranking. Name the payoff in the hook ("wait for the <rarest thing>."); rarity only climbs. Example: every reward of a secret drop ranked worst to best on a ladder of question marks, 59 cuts in 49 s, word-by-word captions (649K views).

**Gameplay gag or fail.** Hook: a moment every player has lived, readable muted. 5-15 s, loops; the game writes the punchline (a death screen, a banner, a stat). Example: text builds word by word over a match ("you know you're a true player when..."), then an open goal missed: 3 shots, 14 s (583K views, 3x usual).

**Clutch or big moment.** Hook: tension, then release. 8-35 s: the tension point, the result, a slow-motion replay of the key half second. Example: a speedrun time promised in the header, a big timer, a face cam with real stress, only the attempts kept (5.7M views).

**Devlog with the dev's voice.** Hook: a person, a stance, visible progress. 20-55 s, voice at 0 s, proof on screen every 2-6 s, gameplay not menus. Example: a weekly Short opens on gameplay with "This week I added <one behavior>", then it plays out: 6 cuts in 51 s, 1.8-3.5M views a part. Also "Day <N> making a <genre> game".

**WIP devlog (scuffed is fine).** Hook: real work, happening now. 20-40 s. Copy a real devlog's beats (a "this week I added..." Short is a good one) with a screen recording of the real dev session: the agent chat and the game changing, each reference beat filled by a moment something changes. Voice-over in the reference's line structure: the developer's own voice, or one that reads the key lines of the chat. Real footage only, captions burned in, no capture mode needed; rough is fine because it is real. The chat on screen is the session, not an AI label: add no "made with AI" text.

**Comment reply (viewer ideas).** Hook: the community's idea, tested, as a numbered series. Example: one viewer suggestion per episode in a single 40 s screen recording, no cuts (2M views on a 2K-follower account).

**Lore short.** Hook: a fact they half know. 20-60 s (100 s for a solved mystery): the claim over the exact thing at 0 s, the stakes by 8 s, a picture change every 2-3 s, the reveal said slower, an open question at the end. Example: a mystery solved through in-game logs, 96 s, 4.2M views on a 196K channel.

**Hero, class or skin showcase.** Hook: choice and identity. 12-30 s, the best ability first, one hero per 1.5-2 s on the beat, a comment prompt at the end. Example: one moment recorded twice and stacked, the new skin in first person on top, the enemy's view below (419K views, 4x usual).

**Trailer cut with a hook.** Hook: a premise nobody has seen, 12 words or fewer by 3 s. 20-22 s on Reels, 40-90 s on YouTube: 2-3 clean gameplay segments on the game's audio, then the name and "Play on summer.games/<slug>" from the kit ("coming soon" if not playable). Example: one tactile action in first person, then a pull back to thousands of the same thing, 13 cuts in 40 s (1.3M views on a 638-subscriber channel).

**Shots that fill a beat:** a real screenshot animated (`makers.cinematic_shot`); before and after, both real; a build in steps, each changing the silhouette; a speed build with an honest clock; a premise card over clean gameplay.

## 4. Footage

Real gameplay wins: on our accounts real footage got 2,500-6,200 views and memes or generated visuals 270-380. Every piece shows at least 2 s of real gameplay; trend swaps end on it.

**Capture to the beat map:** each beat needs its shot, at the beat's length plus a little to trim.

**Choose the look before you capture.** This is where the first pieces failed. Pick the best map, time of day, camera and skins (never the placeholder hero or a bright test level), and write that choice into the kit's style. If no scene looks good, build a filming scene from the game's own assets: a real sky, some fog, lower exposure and bloom, a rim light on the hero. Film with the HUD off whenever you will add text. Never cut menu, store or concept art next to gameplay that does not look like it.

**Reject these frames:** debug screens, blown-out bloom, empty white skies, T-poses, foot sliding, placeholder animations, pop-in, stutter, clipping cameras, missing textures, usernames, notifications, a cursor. No edit saves cheap footage; re-capture.

Sources, best first:
1. **The game's capture mode**, if it has one: HUD toggle, cinematic camera (orbit, follow, low hero angle, slow motion), bots for filming, forced results (a guaranteed legendary), every skin unlocked. If you own the code and it has none, add one behind a flag first; it pays back on every piece.
2. **A web build in headless Chrome with the GPU on** (`--ignore-gpu-blocklist`). Record the game canvas, not the page: `canvas.captureStream(60)` into a `MediaRecorder` (H.264 if offered, about 40 Mbps), with the game's audio tapped from its `AudioContext`. Set the viewport to 1080x1920 and to 1920x1080 for separate takes (device scale 2 for a 4K master), so neither orientation is a crop of the other. Drive inputs from a script and record 3-5 takes per beat. Playwright's own `recordVideo` is soft and silent: use it only to plan shots.
3. **A desktop run in movie mode:** start the game offscreen with `--write-movie shots/frame.png --fixed-fps 60` for lossless frames plus a WAV, frame-exact.
4. **The team's raw clips** from `content.search_library`. Upload what you capture too (`content.upload_begin`), with a one-line description of what happens in it.
5. **Stills:** `engine.capture_gameplay` saves real frames (up to 10) for covers, thumbnails and start frames; hide the HUD first if the game can. `engine.screenshot` and `engine.frame_shot` give a composed frame from the editor.
6. **Shots made from real game art:** `makers.cinematic_shot` (a real frame plus a prompt), `assets.generate_video`, `makers.camera_moves`, `makers.character_turnaround`, from a real screenshot or the kit's pictures, in the game's style, hero on model. At most one per piece, and end on real gameplay.

Capture at 30 fps or more (60 for action you will slow down), at the final aspect. To reframe 16:9 into 9:16, capture at 1440p or higher; never upscale more than 1.35x.

## 5. Edit recipes

You edit with your own tools (ffmpeg, scripts, Remotion if the project has it). The reference's timings, text and voice win; these are the defaults inside each beat.

- **Frame 1 moves.** No idle start, no logo, no title card, no black. Something happens by 1 s.
- **Cut on the first changed frame.** Drop dead frames. No freeze over 0.5 s in the first 1.5 s, and none over 1 s anywhere except the held payoff.
- **Payoff where the reference has it** (usually before 70%), then hold it; short pieces loop, so the last frame leads back into the first.
- **One idea per piece.** Never explain the joke.
- **Text:** big, pure white, bold sans (the kit's font, else Inter Bold), no shadow, no outline, no box behind it unless the kit says so. One text layer at a time (a fixed header, a premise card or a timer is that layer), 7 words or fewer, two sizes at most (title about 7% of the width on vertical). At least 40 px tall on a 1080-wide frame. Put it on a calm part of the frame, never over the game's HUD, a face or the action, and keep it in one place. Wrap a long line to two big lines; never shrink it.
- **Vertical:** per shot, `scale=1080:1920:force_original_aspect_ratio=increase,crop=1080:1920:X:Y` with X and Y on the subject (use 2160x3840 when the source carries it). Move the crop at most once per shot, slowly.
- **Sound:** audio at 0 s and to the last frame; no dead air. The game's audio carries gameplay. Under a voice, music sits 18-22 LU lower or not at all. Build the audio track once for the whole cut, not per segment (per-segment audio drifts out of sync). Loudness -14 LUFS integrated, true peak -1 dBTP or lower.
- **Generated motion in a drawn style:** step it to 12 frames a second; smooth motion reads as fake.
- **Encode:** H.264 High, yuv420p, CRF 17, preset slow, 30 fps (keep 60 if the source has it), AAC 192k, `+faststart`. At least 4000 kbps at 1080p and about 16000 at 4K.

## 6. Per platform

Make a separate render when length, safe zones or aspect differ. One file copied to every platform is not a per-platform cut.

| Platform | Frame | Length | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| TikTok | 1080x1920 (a full-frame 16:9 trailer also works) | 5-15 s for gags and trends, 15-35 s otherwise | No end card: the action line goes over the last action. Link in bio and in the first comment. |
| Instagram Reels | 1080x1920 | 20-22 s, or the trend's length | No end card. The grid crops the cover to the centre 3:4 (y 240-1680): keep the cover text there. |
| YouTube Shorts | 1080x1920 or square | 5-15 s loops, 30-58 s otherwise | Anything wider than square counts as long-form and gets no Shorts reach. Title up to 100 characters, hook in the first 40. No end card. |
| X | 1920x1080 or 1080x1080 | 30-90 s best, 140 s at most | Vertical does badly. Burn in the captions (muted autoplay). Link in a reply, not the post. |
| YouTube long | 1920x1080 or 3840x2160 | 4-15 min | Devlogs and trailers. Title as a search phrase. Thumbnail 1280x720 or larger, 3 words at most. Chapters from 00:00. No music under a voice; ship an SRT. |

**Safe zones on vertical:** keep text and key action out of the top 14%, the bottom 25%, 7% at each side, and the right 13% between 30% and 80% of the height.

## 7. Hooks, captions, sound

**Hooks:** use the reference's hook pattern in our words. Shapes that work: the maker's story with a number ("<N> people. <N> years."); one mystery; one detail, magnified (a second-person premise: "You start as <something tiny>"); a personal, lowercase discovery; naming the payoff. **Weak:** "X but Y" comparisons, "from the studio behind", a logo or title first, a slow establishing shot. On-screen hook: 7 words or fewer, readable in 1.5 s. Spoken hook: 12 words or fewer, finished by 3 s. Rotate openers outside a series.

**Captions:** one dry line, one question that invites an answer, and the words people search for. The game name in plain text. Use 3-5 hashtags on video platforms, the game's tag first, then 1-2 niche tags and at most one trend tag. No em dashes, no emojis, no numbers you cannot source. Avoid kill, blood, murder and death in captions, titles and tags: reach drops.

**First comment:** the play link from the kit. Check it opens on a phone first. If the game is not playable yet, say "coming soon", never "play now".

**Sound:** the game's own audio or a score made for the piece. For a trending sound, cut on its beat using its audio for timing only, strip it, export with game sound, and write the sound and its start time in `suggestedSound` ("<sound name>, start 0:34"); the person adds it in the app.

## 8. Taste bar and self-check

**Why the first pieces failed.** Summer's first game clips passed a measured critic at 7-8 of 10, and the game's maker called them very bad: a bright test map, the placeholder hero, bloom blobs, mismatched menu art, captions on the HUD. Checks catch mistakes, not a cheap look. Taste comes first.

**The taste test.** Put your frame 1 and your best frame next to the game's best art (the kit's character pictures and references, the store art) and next to the reference clip, at phone size. If yours looks cheaper, emptier or smaller, re-capture before you polish. Would a stranger stop on frame 1 with the sound off? Would the team post this on their own account today? If not, it is not done.

**Measured checks (script them; all must pass):**
- Side by side with the reference: every cut within 2 frames, the same text pattern and voice structure, the same length.
- A contact sheet every 0.5 s of every render, that you actually look at.
- Motion in frame 1: no freeze over 0.5 s in the first 1.5 s (`freezedetect`), none over 1 s anywhere except the held payoff.
- Text at least 40 px on a 1080-wide frame, inside the safe zones, clear of the HUD and faces.
- Loudness -14 LUFS (plus or minus 1), true peak -1 dBTP or lower, no silence over 0.5 s (`silencedetect` at -50 dB), audio as long as the video.
- At least 2 s of real gameplay. Short side at least 1080 px. No stretched shot.
- Copy: no AI words, no other game named, nothing that is not live, the link works.
- Different from the last 5 pieces on at least 2 of format, hook, opening frame, sound, length.

**Fresh critic.** Spawn a new subagent with none of your context. Give it the renders, the captions, the reference clip, your beat map and the game's best art. It answers first: does any frame look cheaper than that art (test map, placeholder hero, bloom blobs, empty sky, mismatched menu art, text on the HUD, a debug screen)? Any yes is a rebuild, whatever the score. Then it plays the reference and the piece side by side, beat by beat, watches the first 1.5 s muted, and gives the one idea, whether it stops the scroll, what reads wrong, and a score from 1 to 10 with timestamps. Rebuild below 8, at most twice, and keep the better render. If it still scores under 8, save it with status `draft` and say in `notes` and in your reply line what blocks it. The final score goes in `selfScore`.

## 9. Upload and save

1. For each render and cover: `content.upload_begin` (`fileName`, `contentType`, `size` in bytes) gives an `uploadUrl`; PUT the file there with that content type; then `content.upload_complete` (`uploadId`, `title`, `description` of what happens in it, `tags`, `folder`) gives the item id.
2. `content.save_piece` with `contentGameId`, `title`, `format`, and `variants` (1-5, one per platform: `platform` of `tiktok`, `instagram`, `youtube`, `youtube_long` or `x`; `itemId`; `coverItemId`; `caption`; `title` for YouTube; `hashtags`; `firstComment`; `suggestedSound`). Add `referenceId` (always: the reference you copied), `sourceItemIds`, `gameplaySeconds`, `selfScore`, `notes`, and what Today shows under the player: `why` (`referenceId`, `fitReason`: one line on why it fits today, like the commit you saw, `refStats` with `views`, `likes`, `breakoutRatio`, `postedAt`), `checks` (`hook_seconds`, `min_shot_motion`, `safe_zone`, `loudness_lufs`, `true_peak_db`, `length_seconds`, `gameplay_seconds`, each with the measured `value` and `pass`; never a predicted score), `sideBySideItemId` (a library video: the reference left, yours right, synced), `contactSheetItemId`, `learningIds` (the kit learnings you applied) and `tomorrow` (what you make next). `summer content make` does all of this and reports each stage to its make request (`content.make`, `content.claim_make`, `content.update_make`; `jobs.wait` on `make:<requestId>`). It lands on the team's Today view.
3. Reply with one line and the `reviewUrl`.
4. Keep watching it (section 1, step 7). Feedback arrives on the piece: `needsWork` and `whatToChange`. Revise with `content.update_piece` (pass `expectedRevision`; status `in_review` sends it back). When the team says it is posted, `content.mark_posted`.

## 10. Learnings

Every Change note and Skip reason becomes a learning in the kit by itself (`content.get_kit` `learnings`, with the piece it came from). Read them first on every run, follow each one, and list the ones you applied in `learningIds`. The team removes one with `content.delete_learning`. A data rule you find yourself stays a hypothesis until 3 pieces beat the account's median by 1.5x.

## From a shell

No Summer MCP tools in this session? Run each one as a command; when `summer --version` is missing or below 4.0, use `npx -y summer-engine@latest` in place of `summer`. Fields are flags in kebab-case (`--scene-path res://main.tscn`) or one `--input '<json>'`, and `summer ops describe <op>` prints the exact input. The `summer-cli` skill has the rest.

| In this skill | Command |
|---|---|
| `assets.generate_video`, `summer_assets_generate_video` | `summer assets generate-video` |
| `content.get_kit` | `summer content get-kit` |
| `content.list_games` | `summer content list-games` |
| `content.list_references` | `summer content list-references` |
| `content.make` | `summer content make` |
| `content.make_video` | `summer content make-video` |
| `content.mark_posted` | `summer content mark-posted` |

skills.body:
# /make-game — The orchestration spine

This is the skill that runs end-to-end when a user says "make me a game." It does **not** try to do everything itself. It runs the right specialist skills in the right order with explicit handoffs and a checkpoint between every phase.

**Core principle:** structure beats vibes. A guided pipeline that delegates to focused specialists produces a real game. Off-the-cuff "let me think about it" loops produce three half-finished prototypes. Follow the phases. Don't skip.

## When to use this skill

- User says: "make me a game", "build me a game", "I want to make a [genre]", "let's build a game", "build me a [shape]".
- User has nothing yet and wants the full path from idea → playable.
- User has a vague idea and wants the agent to drive the whole arc.

## When NOT to use this skill

- User has a specific narrow ask ("add jump", "fix this bug", "design the inventory") → use the specific skill, not this orchestrator.
- User already has a working scaffold and wants to iterate → start at the relevant phase below, don't re-run the whole pipeline.
- User says "I want to use a template" → run `browse-templates` first; come back here only if they decide they want a custom build instead.

## Genre playbooks (`references/`)

Distilled blueprints for common genres live in this skill's `references/` folder: architecture, scene tree, collision layers, core-loop code, build order, traps. Each genre is two files — a core file and a systems/polish file. Read the core file during Phase 2 (Plan) so the build plan follows its architecture and build order; read the systems file only when Phase 4 reaches those mechanics. Never load more than the one genre you are building.

| Game | Core | Systems | Root / player / camera |
|---|---|---|---|
| Side-scrolling platformer | `references/2d-platformer.md` | `references/2d-platformer-polish.md` | Node2D / CharacterBody2D / Camera2D follow |
| Horde survivors / bullet heaven | `references/2d-survivors.md` | `references/2d-survivors-progression.md` | Node2D / CharacterBody2D / Camera2D on player |
| Top-down action RPG (also the base for puzzle, grid, tower defense) | `references/2d-rpg.md` | `references/2d-rpg-content.md` | Node2D / CharacterBody2D / Camera2D |
| First-person shooter | `references/3d-fps.md` | `references/3d-fps-systems.md` | Node3D / CharacterBody3D / Camera3D on Head |
| Third-person action / 3D platformer | `references/3d-third-person.md` | `references/3d-third-person-systems.md` | Node3D / CharacterBody3D / SpringArm3D |
| First-person horror | `references/3d-horror.md` | `references/3d-horror-systems.md` | Node3D / CharacterBody3D / Camera3D on Head |

**2D and 2.5D games look painted.** For any 2D or 2.5D request (top-down, RPG, cozy, side-scroller, platformer look), build the world with the `painted-25d-world` skill: a 3D blockout under one fixed orthographic camera, an AI paint-over projected onto the blocks, sprite characters (Node3D / CharacterBody3D / translate-only Camera3D). Use the 2D playbooks above for the core loop, mechanics and build order only, not for the scene tree or art. Do not start a 2D game from a 2D template unless the user asks for that template.

No playbook (racing, sandbox, sim): build fresh through the phases below. The playbooks lean on these system skills — load one when its mechanic comes up: `character-movement`, `camera-rigs`, `combat-basics`, `save-load`, `ui-basics`, `multiplayer-project`.

These rules from the playbooks apply to every genre:

- **2D scales to the viewport.** Set `display/window/stretch/mode = canvas_items` and `stretch/aspect = expand`; UI uses Control anchors; code-positioned nodes compute from `get_viewport_rect().size`. Never hardcode 1920x1080.
- **Playable slice, not tech demo.** Name the core loop in one sentence; every input gets feedback (tween, sound, particle, flash, shake); progression is visible; a restart exists. The bar is "feels good for 30 seconds".
- **Fast first draft when someone is waiting.** The first playable version uses shapes, the palette and any template art, plus at most one or two generated assets the person specifically asked for; generation takes minutes, so it never blocks the first play. Say plainly that it is a first draft to get a feel for the game, that the art is not final, and ask if this is the direction they want. Generate the rest of the art in later passes.
- **A way back to the title.** From inside play, a pause menu or a **Leave** button returns to the title screen without quitting the app.
- **Text the default font can show.** No emoji or symbols (▲ ◀ ★ ♥ ✓) in UI text: they render as boxes with hex codes. Use words or icons; see `ui-basics`.

## The Pipeline

```
  Brainstorm → Plan → Scaffold → Build → Layer → Polish → Verify → Ship
       │        │        │        │        │        │       │       │
       ▼        ▼        ▼        ▼        ▼        ▼       ▼       ▼
  brainstorm  plan   new-project  build-loop   art      vfx    play  export
   -game     (this   browse-      (this skill)  audio          debug -and-
              skill) templates                                       ship
                                                                     
                                  ↓
                         (one mechanic at a time:
                          design-mechanic + scene-composition
                          + gdscript-patterns + play check)
```

Run the phases in order. Between every phase, **stop and confirm with the user before continuing.** The user owns scope decisions; the agent owns execution discipline.

## Phase 1: Brainstorm

**Goal**: turn a vague idea into a 1-page brief.

```
Skill: brainstorm-game
```

That skill asks one question, scopes mechanics, picks an art direction, and writes `.summer/GameSoul.md`. Don't skip this. **The brief is what every later phase reads.**

If the user already has `.summer/GameSoul.md` (check via Read), skip the brainstorm and confirm:

> "Found `.summer/GameSoul.md` — should I build from this brief, or do you want to start over?"

**Checkpoint before continuing:**

> "Brief saved at `.summer/GameSoul.md`. Want me to plan the build?"

## Phase 2: Plan

**Goal**: turn the brief into a concrete checklist of scenes, mechanics, and assets, in priority order.

This phase doesn't have a dedicated skill yet — do it inline. Read `.summer/GameSoul.md` and produce a plan with three sections:

1. **Core scenes** — main scene, level/menu scenes, prefabs the game needs
2. **Core mechanics** — ranked, max 3 (the brief enforces this; respect it)
3. **Cut list** — what's explicitly NOT in scope

If the game has online play, the plan also fixes three product defaults; each one was missed by a real release:

- **Online play is reachable by default.** A new player gets to it from the title without changing a setting. Hiding it behind a setting or a grown-ups gate is the owner's explicit decision, recorded in the plan, and it means someone joins online before every release.
- **Progress is saved by the server.** Online progress goes through authority player data (`summer-player-data`), not only the player's local files.
- **A way back to the title** from inside an online and an offline session.

Save the plan to `.summer/build-plan.md`. Format:

```markdown
# Build plan — <game name>

Source: .summer/GameSoul.md (date)

## Core scenes
- [ ] main.tscn — World + Player + Camera + Light + Floor
- [ ] level_01.tscn — first playable level
- [ ] hud.tscn — health, score
- [ ] (more)

## Core mechanics (in build order)
1. [ ] Movement (FPS / TPS / 2D platformer / etc.)
2. [ ] Primary action (shoot / jump / interact)
3. [ ] Win/lose state

## Cut list (NOT in scope this pass)
- Multiplayer
- Save/load
- Settings menu
- ...
```

**Checkpoint before continuing:**

> "Plan saved. Three core mechanics: movement, primary action, win condition. Anything you want to add or cut before I start building?"

## Phase 3: Scaffold

**Goal**: working project on disk, scene opens in the engine.

If the user said "I want to use a template" earlier, this is just `browse-templates`.

If from scratch:

```
Skill: new-project
```

That picks `empty` vs `3d-basic` based on the GameSoul brief. After the project is created and `summer run` succeeds:

```
Skill: scene-composition
```

To set up the canonical hierarchy for the genre. For 3D action games:

```
World (Node3D)
├── Player (CharacterBody3D)
├── Level (Node3D)
├── Lighting (Node3D)
│   ├── Sun (DirectionalLight3D)
│   └── Environment (WorldEnvironment)
├── HUD (CanvasLayer)
└── GameManager (Node)  # autoload-style, holds win/lose state
```

Build that hierarchy in one `summer_run_script` with the scene's `scenePath` (see `scene-scripting`), not node by node, and end the script with `ctx.save_scene()`. Run `summer_play` once to verify the empty scaffold opens cleanly. If it crashes, run `debug` immediately — do NOT continue building on a broken base.

**Checkpoint before continuing:**

> "Scaffold is in. Empty scene plays clean. Building mechanic 1 of N: <name>. OK?"

## Phase 4: Build (one mechanic at a time)

**Goal**: each mechanic from the plan, fully working, before moving to the next.

For each mechanic in the plan, **in order**:

1. **Design pass**:
   ```
   Skill: design-mechanic
   ```
   Outputs the mechanic spec: input, response, feedback, failure modes, depth, tunables, GDScript stub.

2. **Implement**:
   - Add the nodes: 3 or more scene edits are one `summer_run_script` with `scenePath` (snapshot, script, diff, screenshot); a single tweak is one `summer_set_prop`. Use `scene-composition` if the structure is non-trivial.
   - For movement-class mechanics, prefer the matching pre-built skill: `character-movement`, `fps-controller`, `multiplayer-movement`, etc. Follow the genre playbook's build order when one applies.
   - Write GDScript with `gdscript-patterns` open.

3. **Verify**:
   ```
   Skill: play
   ```
   Then `summer_get_diagnostics`. Clean? Move on. Errors? `debug` until clean. **Do not stack mechanic 2 on top of a broken mechanic 1.**

4. **Checkpoint**:

   > "Mechanic 1 of N working: <name>. <One-line proof: 'WASD moves the player, jump works'>. Building mechanic 2 of N: <name>. OK?"

Repeat until every mechanic in the plan is implemented OR the user calls cut.

## Phase 5: Layer (look + sound)

**Goal**: the game stops looking like a programmer art prototype.

```
Skill: art-direction
```

That writes `.summer/art-bible.md` if it doesn't exist, then guides the lighting / material / palette pass. Use `3d-lighting` for the actual scene work. For the web, check the target first. A summer.games web build (`summer_export_game` with `targets:["web"]`) runs on Summer's WebGPU template, which needs the Forward+ or Mobile renderer. A WebGL 2 target runs the Compatibility renderer only: follow `web-compatibility-look` there, avoid Forward+-only features (SDFGI, SSAO, SSR, volumetric fog), and keep `rendering/renderer/rendering_method` on `gl_compatibility`.

```
Skill: audio-direction
```

Writes `.summer/audio-bible.md` and sets up the audio bus structure. Wires SFX hooks into the mechanics from Phase 4.

Use `asset-strategy` to decide whether to generate assets, search the library, or use primitives. **Public asset library search is free** — encourage it before generation, which costs credits.

**Checkpoint before continuing:**

> "Art and audio direction set. Want me to add a polish pass (juice / VFX / camera shake / hit feedback)?"

## Phase 6: Polish (skip if user wants to ship raw)

**Goal**: the game *feels* good. Hit-flash, screen shake, audio ducking, weight.

```
Skill: game-feel
```

Walks the canonical Summer Engine game-feel stack: hit flash, trauma camera
shake, and audio ducking wired so a single hit fires all three.

```
Skill: tune-performance
```

Only if `summer_get_diagnostics` flags rendering or physics hotspots. Don't optimize prematurely.

## Phase 7: Verify (final QA pass)

**Goal**: the full game runs end-to-end without errors, and the win condition can actually be reached.

1. `play` from main scene.
2. Walk every mechanic from the plan.
3. Hit the win condition (or lose condition).
4. Return to the title from inside play, then start again.
5. Online games: run Local Play (`multiplayer-testing`) and reach online play from the title as a new player, with default settings.
6. `summer_get_diagnostics` clean.
7. `debug` until clean if not.

**Don't skip this even if every mechanic worked individually.** Integration bugs hide between mechanics.

## Phase 8: Ship

```
Skill: export-and-ship
```

Pre-flight checklist (icon, store banners, build config) before producing release builds for the targets in the brief.

Before any version reaches players, run:

```
Skill: release-readiness
```

It checks the file you upload, not the editor: a hosted game's `server.pck` starts its authority scene, `Summer.initialize` passes no hard-coded Game ID, online play is reachable, progress is saved by the server, and players can get back to the title. Then, after publishing, the user joins online with the released version. Report each check as pass, fail, not applicable or not run. Hosted games publish through `multiplayer-publish`; store pages through `publish-your-game`.

If the brief said "jam" or "prototype", skip this phase. If the brief said "game I want to release", run it.

## Anti-Patterns

| Don't | Why |
|---|---|
| Skip the brainstorm because the user said "FPS" | Even with the genre named, you need the scope cut list. Otherwise mechanic 4 quietly sneaks in and the game never ships. |
| Let mechanic 2 start before mechanic 1 is verified clean | Compounding bugs. You'll spend the rest of the session debugging which mechanic broke what. |
| Stack art direction on top of unfinished mechanics | Art changes are reversible only if the underlying scene structure is stable. Get mechanics done first. |
| Treat "polish" as required | If the brief says "jam in 2 days", polish is a cut item. Respect the brief. |
| Run all phases without confirming | The user owns scope. Stop at every checkpoint. |
| Ship online play behind a setting nobody changes | Hosted join is never exercised, so it breaks without anyone noticing. Reachable by default, or the owner joins online before every release. |
| Hard-code a Game ID in `Summer.initialize` | The summer.games bundle has no `gameId`; a different ID fails on the hosted server and every online join times out. Pass no ID. |
| Build a fully featured menu before there's a playable mechanic | Menu work is endless polish; player-loop work is the actual game. Mechanics first. |
| Fall back to "let me try a few things" mid-pipeline | If you don't know what to do, name the phase and ask the user, don't improvise around the structure. |

## What this skill produces (artifacts on disk)

By the end of a successful run, the user has:

- `project.godot` — Summer Engine project
- `main.tscn` — playable main scene
- `.summer/GameSoul.md` — the brief
- `.summer/build-plan.md` — the checklist
- `.summer/art-bible.md` — visual direction
- `.summer/audio-bible.md` — sonic direction
- One `.gd` file per mechanic
- `summer_get_diagnostics` returns clean
- `summer_play` runs end-to-end and the win condition is reachable

## Closing line

When all phases are done:

> "<Game name> is in. <N> mechanics, <playable from main scene to win condition>. <Brief summary of the build>. Want me to package a build (`export-and-ship`) or iterate?"

That's the handoff back to the user.
