## `network/game.gd`

```gdscript
extends RefCounted
## Shared by the client and the authority: ids, streams and shared rules.

const QUEUE := &"courtyard"
const MOTION := &"courtyard.motion"
const CMD := &"courtyard.cmd"
const MATCH := &"courtyard.match"   # one document every player sees
const MINE := &"courtyard.mine"     # one private document per player
const FX := &"courtyard.fx"         # one-off effects, never stored
const MAX_PLAYERS := 8
const COMPOSITION := preload("res://network/composition.tres")

## The authority's sanity bound on movement, in metres per second. Keep it
## above the fastest legitimate speed (walking, jumping, falling).
const MAX_SPEED := 15.0
const ARENA_RADIUS := 40.0


## Adds the World, an Entities root and the Spawner under `parent`. Both sides
## pass their own player archetype; the composition is the same file.
static func build_network(parent: Node, player: SummerEntityArchetype) -> SummerNetworkSpawner:
	var world := SummerNetworkWorld.new()
	world.name = "World"
	parent.add_child(world)
	var entities := Node3D.new()
	entities.name = "Entities"
	parent.add_child(entities)
	var spawner := SummerNetworkSpawner.new()
	spawner.name = "Spawner"
	spawner.network_world_path = NodePath("../World")
	spawner.entities_root_path = NodePath("../Entities")
	spawner.archetypes = [player]
	spawner.player_archetype = &"player"   # one entity per joined player
	spawner.network_composition = COMPOSITION
	parent.add_child(spawner)
	return spawner


## Pose groups are keyed by seat, so a stream needs at most MAX_PLAYERS keys.
static func motion_key(seat: int) -> StringName:
	return StringName("p%d" % seat)


## Seats spawn on a circle. `entity` ties the pose to the player's entity.
static func spawn_pose(seat: int, entity_id: int) -> Dictionary:
	var angle := TAU * float(seat) / MAX_PLAYERS
	return {"entity": entity_id, "position": Vector3(cos(angle) * 4.0, 1.0, sin(angle) * 4.0), "yaw": 0.0}


static func in_bounds(position: Vector3) -> bool:
	return position.is_finite() and Vector2(position.x, position.z).length() <= ARENA_RADIUS \
		and position.y > -10.0 and position.y < 30.0


## Commands and results travel as JSON bytes: a network String holds at most
## 256 bytes.
static func pack(document: Dictionary) -> Dictionary:
	return {"b": JSON.stringify(document).to_utf8_buffer()}


static func unpack(fields: Dictionary) -> Dictionary:
	var parsed: Variant = JSON.parse_string((fields.get("b", PackedByteArray()) as PackedByteArray).get_string_from_utf8())
	return parsed if parsed is Dictionary else {}
```

skills.name: multiplayer-testing
skills.description: Test a Summer multiplayer game with Local Play: several players, bad network, bots, a passing run.
skills.summary: Test a Summer multiplayer game with Local Play: several players, bad network, bots, a passing run.
useWhen: running or testing a Summer multiplayer game locally with several players (Local Play)
testing multiplayer under latency, jitter or packet loss, or with bots
a multiplayer run says ok but nothing networked works, or deciding whether a multiplayer change is done
skills.body:
# /multiplayer-testing — prove it works before saying it works

Step 4 of the multiplayer sequence (`multiplayer` explains the model).

**Local Play** runs a Summer multiplayer game on one machine. It starts the
World's authority scene headless and N clients, and each client joins through
the game's own `Summer.client.join`. No account, server or extra tools are
needed. It can also make the network bad on purpose, which is where
multiplayer bugs show.

## 1. Start Local Play

Pick whichever the session has.

**Summer MCP tools** (they set project settings, then play):

```
summer_project_setting key="summer/local_play/players" value=2
summer_play
summer_get_diagnostics
summer_stop
```

**Editor:** **Debug > Local Multiplayer**, pick the player count, press Play.
The client windows tile side by side.

**Terminal** (`<summer>` is the Summer editor executable). Import once after
adding scripts so their classes register:

```sh
<summer> --headless --path . --import
<summer> --path . --summer-local-play 2 --summer-local-play-timeout 30
```

| Setting | Terminal flag | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `summer/local_play/players` | `--summer-local-play <n>` | Players to start. `-1` uses the queue's `minPlayers`; `0` turns Local Play off |
| `summer/local_play/queue` | `--summer-local-play-queue <name>` | Which `summer.build.json` queue to stand in for (default: the first) |
| — | `--summer-local-play-headless` | Run the clients without windows too |
| — | `--summer-local-play-timeout <s>` | End the session after that many seconds |
| — | `--summer-local-play-smoke` | Headless clients; exit 0 once every client joined and stayed 3 s |
| — | `--summer-local-play-spectators <n>` | Also start spectator clients |
| — | `--summer-local-play-web` | Run the clients in a browser (the game's Web export) |

## 2. Make the network bad

Loopback has no latency, so it hides every timing bug. Always run once with
these settings; they apply to every client:

```
summer_project_setting key="summer/local_play/network/round_trip_msec" value=100
summer_project_setting key="summer/local_play/network/jitter_msec" value=10
summer_project_setting key="summer/local_play/network/loss_percent" value=1
```

Or put them in `project.godot` while testing:

```ini
[summer]

local_play/network/round_trip_msec=100
local_play/network/jitter_msec=10
local_play/network/loss_percent=1
```

Ranges: round trip 0–2000 ms, jitter 0–1000 ms, loss 0–50 %. Each client
prints `NETWORK_EMULATION round_trip_ms=100 ...` when it applies. Try 200 ms
too: that is a player on another continent.

## 3. Read the run

Every output line is prefixed by its process: `[authority]`, `[player-1]`,
`[player-2]`. The last line is the summary:

```text
SUMMER_LOCAL_PLAY_RESULT {"ok":true,"players":2,"network":{...},"processes":[{"label":"authority","script_errors":0,...},{"label":"player-1","joined":true,"script_errors":0,...}],...}
```

A run passes only when **all** of these hold:

- [ ] `"ok":true`, and every process has `"script_errors":0`.
- [ ] The game's own ready lines appear: the authority's, and one per client after its `join` Command (`COURTYARD_AUTHORITY_READY`, `COURTYARD_CLIENT_JOINED` in the Courtyard example). Print one in your game too.
- [ ] No `[SummerNetworkSpawner] cannot attach` warning on any process.
- [ ] No `SCRIPT ERROR` lines.

`"ok":true` alone only proves that clients got seats. If the composition is
invalid, the Spawner logs `cannot attach` as a warning and nothing networked
works, yet every client still counts as joined. The smoke flag
(`--summer-local-play-smoke`) proves the same thing and no more.

With MCP, `summer_get_diagnostics` reports runtime errors from the debugger.
Read it after every play; `summer_get_console` alone misses them.

## 4. Drive the game with bots

To test gameplay without hands, give the game a bot mode. Arguments after
`--` reach every process, and `{client}` becomes 1, 2, ... for players and 0
for the authority:

```sh
<summer> --path . --summer-local-play 2 --summer-local-play-headless --summer-local-play-timeout 20 -- --bot={client}
```

Put the bot in `client/bot.gd`. It presses the same input actions a player
does, so it tests the real controls:

```gdscript
extends Node
## Test bot for Local Play, enabled with `-- --bot={client}`. It presses the
## real input actions. Bot 1 walks to the first coin and collects it; every
## bot prints what it sees, for the test run to check.

const COIN := "0"

var number := 0
var main: Node
var elapsed := 0.0
var step := 0


func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	elapsed += delta
	var me := _own_player()
	if me == null:
		return
	if number == 1 and step == 0:
		var at: Array = main.match_doc.get("coins", {}).get(COIN, [])
		if at.is_empty():
			return
		var to_coin := Vector2(at[0] - me.global_position.x, at[2] - me.global_position.z)
		if to_coin.length() > 0.5:
			_steer(to_coin.normalized())
			return
		_steer(Vector2.ZERO)
		step = 1
		print("BOT_MOVED %s" % me.global_position)
		var collected: Dictionary = await main.collect(COIN)
		print("BOT_COLLECT %s" % JSON.stringify(collected))
	if elapsed > 6.0 and step < 2:
		step = 2
		for node in main.get_node("Entities").get_children():
			if node != me:
				print("BOT_SAW %s" % node.global_position)
		print("BOT_SCORES %s" % JSON.stringify(main.match_doc.get("scores", {})))


func _own_player() -> Node3D:
	for node in main.get_node("Entities").get_children():
		if node.get_script() == preload("res://client/player_owner.gd"):
			return node
	return null


func _steer(direction: Vector2) -> void:
	for action in [&"ui_left", &"ui_right", &"ui_up", &"ui_down"]:
		Input.action_release(action)
	if direction.x > 0.0: Input.action_press(&"ui_right", direction.x)
	if direction.x < 0.0: Input.action_press(&"ui_left", -direction.x)
	if direction.y > 0.0: Input.action_press(&"ui_down", direction.y)
	if direction.y < 0.0: Input.action_press(&"ui_up", -direction.y)
```

Add it from `client/main.gd` only when the argument is there, after the
player has joined:

```gdscript
	# Local Play test bot: `-- --bot={client}` (see multiplayer-testing).
	for arg in OS.get_cmdline_user_args():
		if arg.begins_with("--bot="):
			var bot := preload("res://client/bot.gd").new()
			bot.number = int(arg.trim_prefix("--bot="))
			bot.main = self
			add_child(bot)
```

Then check the lines it prints. The Courtyard bot walks player 1 to a coin
and collects it; player 2 watches:

- [ ] `[player-1] BOT_MOVED` and `[player-2] BOT_SAW` report the same position (the observer is up to 100 ms behind while moving, then equal).
- [ ] `[player-1] BOT_COLLECT {"ok":true...}` and both players print the new score.

Keep bot code in `client/`: files under `test/` or other debug folders are
left out of the players' pack, so the shipped game could not load them.

Headless clients have no real window. Guard calls that need one (mouse
capture, window size) with `DisplayServer.get_name() != "headless"`.

## 5. What Local Play cannot show

- **Hosted-only services** answer with an error code locally: parties,
  friends, World chat, the store, client leaderboards and analytics. Their
  skills list the codes. Make the UI hide or explain them; never crash on them.
- **Matchmaking's accept prompt.** Local Play seats players directly: no
  proposal, one World per queue.
- **A player leaving for good.** A client that quits or calls
  `Summer.client.leave()` only disconnects. `session_disconnected` fires and
  their seat is held. `session_left` arrives when the World ends; hosted, it
  arrives when Summer ends the Session.
- **Which scene the hosted server starts.** Local Play starts the authority
  scene by name. Summer starts the exported `server.pck` with no scene, so a
  server preset without the `summer_authority` feature still passes here and
  then runs the title screen hosted, where every join fails with
  `world_start_timeout`. Run the bundle's `server.pck` with no scene
  (`multiplayer-publish`, step 4d).
- **A wrong Game ID.** Local Play has no hosted identity, so
  `Summer.initialize("some-id")` passes here and fails hosted with
  `game_identity_mismatch`. Call `Summer.initialize()` with no ID; only a
  real online join after publishing proves it.
- **Real devices, real accounts, real distances.** Publish to staging for that
  (`multiplayer-publish`).

Before a version reaches players, run `release-readiness`: it covers these
gaps on the `.zip` you upload.

## Checklist for any multiplayer change

- [ ] Ran Local Play with at least 2 players, and once with 100 ms / 10 ms / 1 %.
- [ ] Every process: no `SCRIPT ERROR`, no `cannot attach`, `script_errors` 0.
- [ ] The game's own ready lines appear for the authority and every client.
- [ ] Your own player responds instantly and never snaps while moving normally.
- [ ] Other players move smoothly and end where their owners are.
- [ ] Shared state matches on every client; private state reaches only its owner.
- [ ] A refused Command changes nothing and shows its reason.

## Common mistakes

| Don't | Do | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Test only on loopback | Add round trip, jitter and loss | Latency bugs are invisible at 0 ms |
| Read `"ok":true` as success | Also check your ready lines, `cannot attach` and `script_errors` | A broken composition still joins |
| Read only `summer_get_console` | `summer_get_diagnostics` after each play | Runtime errors live in the debugger |
| Put bot or test code under `test/` and load it from the game | Keep the bot in `client/`, enabled by `--bot` | Debug folders are left out of the players' pack |
| Wait for `session_left` in a local test | Watch `session_disconnected` | Local Play ends Sessions only when the World ends |
| Skip the import pass after adding scripts | `<summer> --headless --path . --import` first | New classes are unknown until imported |

## Next

`multiplayer-publish`: export the summer.games bundle and upload it as a Build.

<!-- shell-commands: generated from the operation catalog by npm run generate:registry; do not edit by hand -->
## From a shell

No Summer MCP tools in this session? Run each one as a command; when `summer --version` is missing or below 4.0, use `npx -y summer-engine@latest` in place of `summer`. Fields are flags in kebab-case (`--scene-path res://main.tscn`) or one `--input '<json>'`, and `summer ops describe <op>` prints the exact input. The `summer-cli` skill has the rest.

| In this skill | Command |

| `summer_get_console` | `summer engine get-console` |
| `summer_get_diagnostics` | `summer engine get-diagnostics` |
| `summer_play` | `summer engine play` |
| `summer_project_setting` | `summer engine project-setting` |
| `summer_screenshot` | `summer engine screenshot` |
| `summer_stop` | `summer engine stop` |

skills.summary: Generate a music track: game loops of 30s or more with a loop point, or linear cinematic cues.
useWhen: generating a looped or cinematic music track — main theme, boss music, title screen, exploration loop, combat track
a game has no music yet or needs a new track for a level, a cutscene, or the credits
skills.body:
# /music-track — Generate a Loop or Cinematic Music Track

## Overview

ElevenLabs Music renders a track from a prompt. Summer clamps the requested length to **3–600 seconds** before sending it, so anything outside that range is silently pulled to the nearest bound. Quality depends on prompt specificity: tempo (BPM), key, instrumentation, mood, structural cue. "Epic orchestral" returns generic stock music. "85 BPM, D minor, solo cello and detuned upright piano, sparse, melancholic, no drums, 4/4" returns a usable score for a melancholic exploration scene.

This skill produces one track aligned with the audio bible's music style and dynamic music plan, then wires it as an `AudioStreamPlayer` on the `Music` bus with a marked loop point if it's a loop, or as a linear cinematic stream if it's a one-shot.

## When to use

- Looped track for a level, biome, menu, or game state (calm / tension / combat).
- Cinematic linear track for an intro, ending, boss reveal, or cutscene.
- Replacing a placeholder loop with on-bible music.

## When NOT to use

- Short stings / event punctuation (<5s) → use `sound-effect` with class `Stinger`.
- Adaptive layered stems with state-driven crossfades → `adaptive-music`.
- Ambient bed with no melody → `ambient-bed`.

## Steps

### 1. Read the audio bible

```
Read .summer/audio-bible.md
```

The bible names the primary style, tempo range, key center, time signature, and the dynamic music model. This skill writes prompts that respect those numbers.

If no bible exists:

> No `.summer/audio-bible.md`. Music without an audio bible drifts into stock-library territory. Run `/audio-direction` first, or I can ship a one-off with explicit defaults — your call.

### 2. Identify the track's role

Ask if not obvious:

> Which slot in the dynamic music plan? Calm exploration, tension, combat, boss, victory, menu, ending, or one-off cutscene?

Each slot has different rules:

| Slot | Tempo | Energy | Instrumentation density | Loop or linear |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Calm exploration | bible low end (e.g. 70–90) | Low | Sparse | Loop, ≥45s |
| Tension | mid (e.g. 90–110) | Medium, no drums or sparse pulse | Adds one instrument | Loop, ≥45s |
| Combat | high (e.g. 120–150) | High, full drums | Full | Loop, ≥45s |
| Boss | high or low-and-menacing | Distinct from combat | Distinct, named instrument | Loop, ≥60s |
| Victory sting | n/a | Resolution | n/a | Linear, 4–8s (use SFX skill instead) |
| Menu / title | bible mid | Atmospheric | Anchor instrument | Loop, ≥30s |
| Cutscene | varies | Linear arc | Varies | Linear, 60–180s |
| Ending | varies | Linear arc with resolution | Varies | Linear, 60–300s |

### 3. Build the prompt — tempo + key + instrumentation + mood + structural cue

Prompts that work:

```
85 BPM, D minor, 4/4, solo cello and detuned upright piano, sparse, melancholic
exploration loop, no drums, gentle reverb, even dynamics, 60s

128 BPM, D dorian, 4/4, full orchestral combat, low brass ostinato, taiko drums
on 1 and 3, strings tremolo, urgent, no melodic resolution, 60s loop

90 BPM, A minor, 6/8, lo-fi exploration, vintage Rhodes electric piano,
tape hiss, warm bass, soft brushed snare, no vocals, 45s loop

70 BPM, F minor, 4/4, ambient menu loop, pad layer, distant choir, single
piano motif every 8 bars, no drums, 30s loop with seamless return

110 BPM, C minor harmonic, 4/4, dark synthwave boss intro, gated reverb snare,
arpeggiated bass synth, lead saw on melody, builds to cymbal swell at 0:50,
linear 60s, ends on sustained pad
```

Prompts that DON'T work (and why):

| Bad prompt | Failure mode |
|---|---|
| `epic orchestral combat music` | No tempo, no key, no instrumentation. Generic stock. |
| `Hollow Knight style track` | The model can't reference IPs and won't try to clone style words. |
| `hopeful but sad menu music with strings and stuff` | "Strings and stuff" is vague; model picks the wrong section. |
| `something for the boss fight` | No tempo, no key, no mood vector. Random. |
| `loop` (just the word) | No structure. Returns 30s of music that doesn't loop. |

### 4. Tempo, key, instrumentation specifics that matter

**Tempo (BPM)** — name a single number, not a range. Music model interprets ranges as mid-point with drift. `85 BPM` is better than `80–90 BPM`.

**Key** — name mode (`D minor`, `D dorian`, `D natural minor`, `C minor harmonic`). The bible's modulation rules go here: combat tracks shift to dorian, calm tracks to natural minor.

**Instrumentation** — name 2–4 specific instruments, not sections. `solo cello` not `strings`. `upright piano` not `keys`. `Rhodes electric piano` not `electric piano`. The model's vocabulary is closer to a session musician's than a producer's.

**Mood** — concrete adjectives anchored to motion: `melancholic and slow`, `urgent and driving`, `triumphant and rising`. Avoid genre adjectives like `epic`, `chill`, `hype`.

**Structural cue** — for linear tracks, name the arc: `builds at 0:30 to a hit at 0:50, decays`. For loops, name the cell: `4-bar phrase repeats, instrument swap every 8 bars`.

### 5. Loop vs cinematic decision

| Choose loop when | Choose linear when |
|---|---|
| The slot plays for an unbounded time (level, menu, exploration) | The slot has a known length (cutscene, intro, ending) |
| Player attention is on gameplay | Player attention is on the music |
| You want to layer adaptive stems on top later | The arc is the point |

For loops: generate **≥30s, prefer 45–60s**. Shorter loops are recognized as repetition within 90s of play and become annoying. The bible's "no state stays >90s without variation" rule means even a 60s loop should contain internal variation (instrument swap on alternating cycles).

For linear: generate **≥60s for cutscenes, up to 300s for endings**. Ask for one rendered piece rather than splicing; the model handles long arcs.

### 6. Confirm and call

Show the prompt:

> Prompt:
> `85 BPM, D minor, 4/4, solo cello and detuned upright piano, sparse, melancholic exploration loop, no drums, gentle reverb, 60s loop`
> Duration 60s. This uses credits. Generate?

The `music` capability reads the description from **`prompt`**, not `text` — the mirror image of `sound_effects`. Without `prompt` the call is refused (`prompt_required`).

```
assets.generate_audio({
  capability: "music",
  prompt: "85 BPM, D minor, 4/4, solo cello and detuned upright piano, sparse, melancholic exploration loop, no drums, gentle reverb, 60s loop",
  durationSeconds: 60
})
// Then: summer_import_from_url(url: "<asset.fileUrl>", path: "res://audio/music/calm_exploration.mp3")
```

`durationSeconds` is clamped to 3–600, and a longer track costs more: `dryRun: true` returns the `estimate` in credits first. Music comes back as MP3 (`audio/mpeg`), so a `.mp3` target path is correct.

### 7. Mark the loop point in Summer Engine

ElevenLabs Music does not return a loop-clean cut. You must mark the loop point
in Summer Engine's Import dock so playback returns to the loop point on
completion, not to 0:00.

The MP3 importer exposes exactly five options — `loop`, `loop_offset`, `bpm`, `beat_count`, `bar_beats`. There is **no `loop_mode`** on MP3 or OGG; `loop_mode` belongs to the WAV importer, where it is spelled `edit/loop_mode`.

In `audio/music/calm_exploration.mp3.import`:

```
[params]
loop = true
loop_offset = 0.0
```

If the start has a fade-in but the body is loopable, set `loop_offset = 4.0` (4 seconds of intro skipped on loop, plays full track first time). `bpm` + `beat_count` + `bar_beats` are what you set if you want beat-synced transitions later — see `adaptive-music`.

For seamless looping, the cleaner option is to ask the model to generate a cell (one bar / one phrase) and concatenate; or generate at 60s and trust the model's structural cue. Crossfade looping in code is the practical fallback (step 9).

### 8. Wire it as `AudioStreamPlayer` on the `Music` bus

One script adds the player with its settings; `scenePath` is the exact scene to change:

```
summer_run_script(scenePath="res://main.tscn", source="""
func run(ctx):
    ctx.add_node("AudioStreamPlayer", "MusicCalm", null, {
        "stream": load("res://audio/music/calm_exploration.mp3"),
        "bus": "Music",
        "volume_db": -8.0,
        "autoplay": true,
    })
    ctx.save_scene()
""")
```

Music is `AudioStreamPlayer` (not 2D / 3D) — non-positional. The bible's `Music -8 dB` mix sits the music behind SFX where it belongs.

### 9. Crossfade-loop pattern (no marked loop point)

If the loop click bothers the user, crossfade two players. Set `loop = false` in the import file first, so each player stops at the end.

```gdscript
# scripts/audio/MusicLoopCrossfade.gd
extends Node
@export var stream: AudioStream
@export var fade := 1.0
@export var volume_db := -8.0
var _players: Array[AudioStreamPlayer] = []
var _current := 0

func _ready() -> void:
	for i in 2:
		var p := AudioStreamPlayer.new()
		p.stream = stream
		p.bus = "Music"
		p.volume_db = volume_db
		add_child(p)
		_players.append(p)
	_players[0].play()

func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	var a := _players[_current]
	if not a.playing or a.get_playback_position() < stream.get_length() - fade:
		return
	_current = 1 - _current
	var b := _players[_current]
	b.volume_db = -80.0
	b.play()
	var t := create_tween().set_parallel()
	t.tween_property(a, "volume_db", -80.0, fade)
	t.tween_property(b, "volume_db", volume_db, fade)
	t.chain().tween_callback(a.stop)
```

The next player starts `fade` seconds before the current one ends and the two cross over, so the seam is never heard.

## Reference card — prompts by slot

```
Calm explore (folk):    78 BPM, D minor, 6/8, fingerpicked acoustic guitar,
                        upright bass on 1, soft hand percussion, no melody on
                        first 8 bars, 60s loop

Tension (orchestral):   95 BPM, D dorian, 4/4, low strings sustained, single
                        timpani roll every 8 bars, sparse french horn motif,
                        no drums, 60s loop

Combat (orchestral):    140 BPM, D dorian, 4/4, taiko drums on 1 and 3,
                        ostinato low brass, strings tremolo, urgent and driving,
                        no melodic resolution, 60s loop

Boss (synthwave):       110 BPM, C minor harmonic, 4/4, gated snare, arpeggio
                        bass synth, lead saw on melody, builds at 0:50,
                        linear 60s

Menu (lo-fi):           70 BPM, F minor, 4/4, vintage Rhodes, tape hiss,
                        soft brushed snare, single piano motif every 8 bars,
                        45s loop

Cutscene (cinematic):   varies tempo, D minor, 4/4, solo piano opens,
                        strings enter at 0:20, full orchestra at 0:50,
                        decay to solo piano at 1:30, linear 120s
```

## Anti-patterns

- **Genre adjectives only.** `epic`, `chill`, `hype` — meaningless.
- **Naming a game or composer.** Model won't replicate; use ingredients.
- **Loop shorter than 30s.** Recognized as repetition fast.
- **Music on `Master` bus at 0 dB.** Buries SFX. Use `Music` bus at `-8 dB`.
- **Generating before reading the bible.** Style drift.
- **Skipping the loop-mark step.** Music returns to 0:00 with a click on every loop.

## Edge cases

- **Clip is 50s but you wanted 60s.** Either regenerate or extend by overlap-crossfading the last 5s onto the start in an audio editor.
- **Loop click on every cycle.** Use the crossfade pattern in step 9.
- **Clip is too long.** Trim the tail in the import dock with `loop_offset`, or in an audio editor.
- **Track sounds nothing like the references.** Re-read the bible; the prompt may be missing the anchor instrument. Add it explicitly.
- **Track has unexpected vocals.** Add `no vocals, instrumental only` to the prompt.

## Without Summer Engine

In a session without Summer Engine tools (the assets profile; the `summer-assets` skill has the whole loop), do steps 1-6 and skip steps 7-9 (loop point, `AudioStreamPlayer`, crossfade script). Save the file where the person asked with `out` (the `summer-assets` skill says how), and tell them the path and format. For a loop track, tell them it is made to loop.

## Fallback (no MCP)

Print the prompt and instruct the user to run via the Summer dashboard, then `summer_import_from_url` the rendered MP3.

## Handoff

> Track `calm_exploration.mp3` wired to `Game/MusicCalm` on the `Music` bus, autoplay on. Next:
> - Mark the loop point in the import dock if the bible calls for looped playback.
> - Generate the tension and combat counterparts with `/music-track` again.
> - To wire state-driven crossfades between calm / tension / combat, run `/adaptive-music`.

## See also

- `audio-direction` — defines style, tempo, key, model
- `adaptive-music` — wiring stems to game state
- `sound-effect` — short stings
- `ambient-bed` — non-melodic location bed

skills.body:
# navigate-summer — land the user exactly where they want to look

## Overview

Summer has two surfaces the user looks at: **summerengine.com** (Studio, games, billing, templates, guides, docs) and the **Summer Engine editor** (scenes, nodes, docks). `studio.open` — the same behavior as `summer open <target>` in a shell, run by the Summer MCP on this computer — takes an intent ("billing", "my games", "the scene I'm editing", "res://player.gd") and opens the exact page or panel, or prints the URL / engine op so you can hand it over. The **product map** reference (`summer_docs_read` id `reference/product-map`) is the full table of destinations with their intent phrases, required context, and what the user will see.

A call written `studio.open({...})` is `summer_call({ op: "studio.open", input: {...} })` (3.x name: `summer_open`). The fields below are in the answer's `result`.

Rigid skill: follow the rules below exactly.

## The one decision: open a surface, or act?

| The user wants to… | Do |
|---|---|
| **see / check / decide** — plan and billing (money), their published games and releases, usage, pricing, the MCP setup guide for their agent, docs, the scene or node you just built ("show me") | **Open the surface** with `studio.open` |
| **get a result** — add a node, set a property, import an asset, run the game, publish | **Act through Summer tools** (mutation tools, `summer_play`, `store.publish`); do not click through the editor by hand to do what a tool does |
| **both** ("add a camera and show me") | act first, then open the scene / select the node so the user sees the result |

Never open a browser or switch the editor's tab as a side effect of building. Opening a page or panel is a user-visible action — do it because the user asked to look, and say what will open before it opens. Playing the game and taking screenshots to check your own work is different: that is allowed and expected (`summer_play`, then `summer_screenshot` or `summer_frame_shot`).

## How to call it

1. **Resolve first when unsure.** `studio.open({ target: "change my plan", open: false })` returns the matched target, the URL (and `login_url` if login is required), or the engine op — nothing opens. If `action` is `ambiguous`, pick from `matches` and call again with the `id`.
2. **Open.** `studio.open({ target: "billing" })` opens the browser at Studio → Billing. `studio.open({ target: "scene", params: { path: "res://levels/level_1.tscn" } })` opens the scene in the running editor. `studio.open({ target: "node", params: { node: "Player/Camera3D" } })` selects the node. `studio.open({ target: "res://player.gd" })` routes by extension.
3. **Fill the slots the target declares.** `game` needs `params.gameId` (and an optional `section` such as `builds`, `releases`, `store-page`, `analytics`); `mcp-guide` takes `params.guide` as an agent name (`cursor`, `claude-code`, `codex`, `gemini`, …); `profile` takes `username`; `changelog` takes `version`.
4. **List when you do not know the id.** `studio.open({})` returns every target with `surface`, `status`, and `requires`. In a shell: `summer open --list`.

## Read the result honestly

- `action: "opened"` — say what opened, in one line ("Opened Studio → Billing in your browser.").
- `logged_in: false` with `login_url` — the login page opened with `returnUrl` set; tell the user the destination loads after sign-in.
- `action: "engine_not_running"` — nothing opened. Tell the user to start Summer Engine (`summer run <project>`) or open the project in the desktop app, then offer to retry. Do not fall back to editing files.
- `action: "unsupported"` (`failure_reason: engine_lacks_op`) — this Summer Engine build cannot open that surface (it predates the `Navigate` op, or does not advertise that id). Say so plainly, tell the user to update Summer Engine, and describe what to open by hand. Never claim it opened.
- `action: "ambiguous"` — show the top matches by title and ask, or pick the obvious one and say which you picked.
- `action: "not_found"` — the intent is not a Summer destination (or a `res://` path tried to escape the project). Do not invent a URL; the tool only opens summerengine.com and its subdomains.
- `action: "open_failed"` — this machine could not launch a browser (headless, no display). Nothing opened; paste the `url` for the user.
- `action: "blocked_origin"` — the configured gateway is not a Summer origin; nothing opened. Tell the user to check `gateway.url` / `SUMMER_GATEWAY_URL`.

## When to hand over a link instead

Use `open: false` (CLI: `--print`) and paste the `url` (or `login_url`) when the session has no browser (headless, remote, CI), when the user asked for a link, or when opening would interrupt what the user is doing. A link the user clicks is always acceptable; a browser window that appears unasked is not.

## Editor targets

The editor owns its own table of destinations (the `Navigate` op) and tells the tool which ids it can open. `studio.open({})` lists every editor id with `availability`: `available` (Navigate op), `legacy` (an older engine serving it through its original op), `unavailable` (update Summer Engine), `unknown` (engine not running). Ids: `scene` (default = the project's main scene), `main-scene`, `node`, `script` (with `line`), `file`, `files`, `scene-tree`, `inspector`, `import-dock`, `signals-dock`, `changes-dock`, `screen-2d/3d/script/game/assetlib`, `viewport-show/hide`, `assistant`, `project-settings`, `editor-settings`, `output`, `debugger`, `editor-window`. On a legacy engine, `script` opens without taking focus — mention it if the user does not see it.

## Anti-patterns

- Opening `billing` or `pricing` when the user asked about a **feature**, not money.
- Opening the scene in the editor **before** the change landed ("show me" comes after the mutation and its screenshot).
- Guessing a `gameId`. Open `my-games` and let the user pick, or read the id from a URL they gave you.
- Describing a page you did not open. If `ok` is false, the user saw nothing.

Fields are flags in kebab-case (`--scene-path res://main.tscn`) or one `--input '<json>'`, and `summer ops describe <op>` prints the exact input. The `summer-cli` skill has the rest.

starting a Summer Engine project with no template, only a name, ready for an empty main scene
skills.body:
# /new-project — Scaffold a fresh empty project

Use this when the user wants a blank project instead of a template.

## When to use this skill

- "Let's start a new project."
- "I want to make a [game type] from scratch."
- "Blank project."
- "Empty project."
- "I don't want a template, just a blank starting point."

## When NOT to use this skill

- "Show me templates" / "use a template" → `browse-templates`.
- "Make me a game" with a defined idea → run `brainstorm-game` first to scope, then come back here once the user knows what they want.
- "I have an existing Godot project I want to import" → not this skill; have the user run `summer open <path>` directly.

## Steps

### 1. Ask the project name

One question, no menu:

> "What do you want to call your project?"

Default: `my-game`. If they say "anything is fine" or similar, use `my-game` and move on. The directory name is reversible — they can always rename.

### 2. Pick the starting scene

Two built-in options:

- `empty` — root `Node3D` only. Pure blank canvas. Best for: experimentation, when the user knows exactly what they want to build.
- `3d-basic` — root `Node3D` with a procedural sky on a `WorldEnvironment`, a sun with soft shadows, a tinted ground, one hero mesh and a `Camera3D` that frames it. Best for: first-time users who want something they can press Play on.

If you're not sure which fits, ask:

> "Empty (just a root node) or 3d-basic (camera, light, and a floor — you can press play immediately)?"

If the user has clearly invoked `brainstorm-game` already and the brief calls for 3D, default to `3d-basic` and mention you did. If 2D or 2.5D, use `empty`, keep its `Node3D` root and build the world with `painted-25d-world` (a painted 3D blockout under a fixed orthographic camera with sprite characters).

### 3. Create and open it

One command creates the project and opens it. When Summer Engine is missing it also installs it (about 660 MB): ask the user first, and pass `--yes` only with their OK (without it nothing is installed):

```
summer dev --yes 3d-basic my-game
```

or `summer dev --yes empty my-game`. It writes `project.godot` and the chosen `main.tscn` (no network call for these two), opens the editor and waits until it answers.

No shell in this session (a chat app)? Call `projects.create_local` with `template` and `name`, then `projects.open_local` with its `projectPath` (and `install: true` only after the user said yes to installing the engine).

Confirm the project loaded with `summer_get_project_context`. If it fails, run `summer doctor` and surface the failure to the user.

### 4. Don't keep going automatically

After scaffolding, **stop and let the user direct.** A common mistake: fire `fps-controller` or `design-mechanic` automatically because "now we make a game." Wait. The user might want to:

- Brainstorm what to build (`brainstorm-game`)
- Set the visual direction (`art-direction`)
- Jump straight into a known mechanic (`design-mechanic`)
- Build a specific controller (`fps-controller`)

Ask: "Project is open. What do you want to build?"

## Anti-patterns

| Don't | Why |
|---|---|
| Skip the name question and use `my-game` silently | The user has opinions about the directory name. Two seconds of asking saves a `mv` later. |
| Use `summer create 3d-basic` for a 2D game | Its light and floor fight the painted look. Use `empty` and follow `painted-25d-world`. |
| Default to a community template | That's `browse-templates`. This skill is specifically for "blank canvas." |
| Continue into `fps-controller` automatically | Most users want to brainstorm or set art direction first. Stop and ask. |
| Run this when the user is in an existing project | Check `summer status` or `summer_get_project_context` first. If a project is already open, the user probably wanted to modify it, not create a new one. |

## Edge cases

- **Engine not running** → that's fine. `summer dev` (or `projects.open_local`) starts it; `summer create` alone doesn't need it.
- **User wants 2D or 2.5D** → use `empty`, keep the `Node3D` root and follow `painted-25d-world`. Use a `Node2D` root only when the user asks for a classic 2D tile or pixel game.
- **Directory exists** → a folder that already holds `project.godot` is just opened; one with other files is refused. Ask for a different name; don't try to overwrite.

## Closing

End with: "Project `<name>` is created and open. What do you want to build first?"

skills.name: organic-model
skills.description: Generate organic 3D shapes (trees, rocks, mushrooms, plants, crystals) where irregularity looks natural.
skills.summary: Generate organic 3D shapes (trees, rocks, mushrooms, plants, crystals) where irregularity looks natural.
useWhen: generating organic shapes — trees, rocks, mushrooms, coral, bushes, alien plants, vines, crystals, fruit, bones
a level needs vegetation, rocks, or other natural shapes where irregularity reads as realism
skills.body:
# Organic Model — Easy-Mode 3D Generation

Organic shapes (trees, rocks, mushrooms, coral, alien flora, crystals, vines, bones) are **the most forgiving category for AI 3D generation**. Lumps look natural. Asymmetry looks natural. Smoothing-group artifacts read as bark texture. The "melted" look that ruins vehicles and characters is fine on a mossy boulder.

This is the cheapest, fastest way to fill out a scene, and the first choice when the user says "this scene feels empty". The failure rate is the lowest of any 3D-asset family.

Backing operation: `assets.generate_3d` (it answers with a job: `jobs.wait` until it finishes). Default `hunyuan` works well here, but `trellis` is faster and the quality difference is hard to see on organic shapes. Pick `trellis` when generating many at once.

## When to use

- "Make me a pine tree."
- "Generate five different rocks I can scatter."
- "I need glowing mushrooms for the cave."
- "Fill this forest scene with foliage."
- "Alien plants for the planet surface."
- "Coral for the underwater level."
- The user wants visual density quickly and cheaply.

## When NOT to use

- Character (humanoid, even if "tree-person") → `character-model` (rigging matters).
- Vehicle, weapon, hard-surface object → `prop-model` or `vehicle-model`.
- Tileable ground (grass field, sand) → `asset-strategy` Pipeline 2 (textures, not meshes).
- Animated organic (Venus fly trap that opens, breathing pod) → generate static here, animate in-engine with bones or shape keys.
- A single hero-tree centerpiece (Yggdrasil, the One Tree) — generate via `prop-model` with higher polycount and detail attention.

## Polycount targets

Organic geometry tolerates aggressive polycount cuts because the silhouette is irregular — viewers can't spot poly-count drops the way they spot a low-poly cylinder.

| Use case | Tris | Pass via |
|---|---|---|
| Hero tree (mid-distance, prominent) | 4k–8k | `targetPolycount: 6000` |
| Background tree (forest filler) | 1k–3k | `targetPolycount: 2000` |
| Distant tree (use billboard imposter) | 200–500 | `targetPolycount: 400` |
| Large rock / boulder | 800–2000 | `targetPolycount: 1500` |
| Small organic (mushroom, fruit, crystal) | 300–1000 | `targetPolycount: 600` |
| Vine / branch decoration | 200–500 | `targetPolycount: 400` |

Generating a forest? Make 3 hero trees + 5 background trees + 3 rocks at low polycount, then scatter via `MultiMeshInstance3D` for hundreds of copies at near-zero rendering cost.

## Steps

### 1. Search before generating

```
assets.search({ query: "<organic type>", assetType: "3d_model", scope: "all" })
```

### 2. Build the prompt

Pattern: `<species> + <state/condition> + <key features> + isolated suffix`. Organic prompts are shorter than prop prompts — the model already knows what a tree looks like.

| Goal | Prompt that works |
|---|---|
| Pine tree | `A tall pine tree with dense green needles and a straight trunk, slight lean. Game asset, stylized low-poly game art, white background, isolated object.` |
| Oak tree | `A wide oak tree with sprawling branches and seasonal autumn leaves in orange and red. Game asset, stylized, white background, isolated object.` |
| Boulder | `A large mossy boulder, irregular weathered surface, patches of green moss on top. Game asset, stylized, white background, isolated object.` |
| Glowing mushroom | `A cluster of three bioluminescent mushrooms on a small mossy base, pale cyan glow, translucent caps. Game asset, stylized, white background, isolated object.` |
| Alien plant | `An alien spiral plant with tendril-like fronds, deep purple with glowing pink tips, growing from a bulbous base. Game asset, stylized, white background, isolated object.` |
| Coral cluster | `A branching coral cluster, bright orange and pink, sea-fan shapes, multiple branches. Game asset, stylized, white background, isolated object.` |
| Crystal | `A jagged amethyst crystal cluster growing from a stone base, deep purple with translucent facets. Game asset, stylized, white background, isolated object.` |
| Vine | `A hanging jungle vine with broad green leaves and small white flowers, ~2 meter length. Game asset, stylized, white background, isolated object.` |

Organic prompts that DON'T work:

| Bad prompt | Failure mode |
|---|---|
| `a tree` | Returns a generic tree, but inconsistent species across regenerations — the scene looks chaotic. Always specify species. |
| `a forest` | Returns one fused mesh of multiple trees → impossible to scatter. Generate one tree, scatter via MultiMeshInstance3D. |
| `realistic tree with photoreal bark` | Realistic = expensive polycount, ugly when stylized assets surround it. Match scene style. |
| `a tree on a hill` | The hill becomes geometry. Always say `isolated object`. |

### 3. Confirm and call

> About to generate `pine_tree_01` via `trellis`, target ~2k tris, ~30s. This uses credits. OK?

For batch generation, batch the confirmation:

> About to generate 3 trees + 3 rocks + 5 mushrooms (11 generations, ~5 min). All low-poly via `trellis`. OK?

`dryRun: true` on one call gives its credits (`estimate.credits`) for the batch confirmation. Start every generation of the batch first, then wait on the jobs.

```
assets.generate_3d({
  prompt: "A tall pine tree with dense green needles and a straight trunk, slight lean. Game asset, stylized low-poly game art, white background, isolated object.",
  model: "trellis",
  targetPolycount: 2000
})
jobs.wait({ jobId: "<job.id>", timeoutSeconds: 50 })   // again until finished; result.assetId
assets.get({ assetId: "<assetId>" })
summer_import_asset_by_id(assetId="<assetId>", path="res://assets/organic/pine_tree_01.glb")
```

### 4. Generate variation, not duplication

If the user wants "five rocks", don't generate one rock and copy it five times in the scene — generate five subtly different prompts:

```
"A medium boulder, mossy granite, rounded shape"
"A medium boulder, weathered limestone, sharp jagged edges"
"A medium boulder, dark basalt, flat-topped"
"A medium boulder, sandstone, layered horizontal striations"
"A medium boulder, mossy granite, tall narrow shape"
```

Then scatter all five with random rotation. Five unique meshes + rotation = looks like 50 unique rocks.

### 5. Wire into the scene

| Use case | Wiring | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Single hero tree, mid-scene | `MeshInstance3D` under `Node3D` | One per scene; nothing fancy |
| Forest scatter (50+ trees) | `MultiMeshInstance3D` with one mesh ref | Single draw call for all instances |
| Foliage variety (3 species) | One `MultiMeshInstance3D` per species | Each species is one draw call |
| Distant trees | Billboard imposter (Sprite3D with a tree image) | Switch from mesh to billboard at ~50m via LOD |
| Rocks with collision | `StaticBody3D` parent + `CollisionShape3D` (ConcaveShape from mesh) | Only for rocks the player can walk into |
| Rocks without collision (background) | Just `MeshInstance3D` | Most distant rocks don't need it |

**Hero tree:**

```
summer_instantiate_scene(scenePath="res://main.tscn", parent="./World/Forest", scene="res://assets/organic/oak_tree.glb", name="HeroOak")
summer_save_scene(scenePath="res://main.tscn")
```

A `.glb` cannot be assigned to `MeshInstance3D.mesh`. An imported `.glb` is a scene, not a `Mesh` — on the shipped 4.6.1 binary `ResourceLoader.get_recognized_extensions_for_type("Mesh")` returns `["tres", "mesh", "res"]`, with no `glb`. `summer_instantiate_scene` adds it as a child in one op. (For the `MultiMeshInstance3D` path below you do need a real `Mesh`: pull it out of the instantiated scene's `MeshInstance3D` in script, or save it as a `.tres`.)

Every scene-mutating tool takes an explicit `scenePath`; node paths are relative to that scene's root (`./`).

**Forest scatter (MultiMesh):** create a `MultiMeshInstance3D`, assign a `MultiMesh` resource referencing the tree mesh, set `instance_count` to e.g. 100, and populate `set_instance_transform()` from a script with random positions + rotations. See `scene-composition` for the scatter pattern.

### 6. LOD and billboards

For dense forests, the cheapest fix beyond MultiMesh is the billboard imposter:

1. Generate the tree mesh once at high polycount.
2. Render it from one angle to a transparent PNG (an `EditorScript` can capture a viewport).
3. Use that PNG as a `Sprite3D` with `billboard = enabled`.
4. Swap from `MeshInstance3D` to `Sprite3D` at ~50m camera distance with `visibility_range_end` on the mesh and `visibility_range_begin` on the sprite (both on `GeometryInstance3D`), or a custom LOD script.

In a 200-tree forest, only the ~10 closest trees need to be real meshes; the other 190 can be billboards.

## Anti-patterns

- **Generating "a forest" as one prompt.** Returns a single fused mesh — useless for placement. Always one species per generation, then scatter.
- **Regenerating the same species 5 times for variety.** Generate 5 *different* species/states/colors for true variety; identical regenerations don't differ enough.
- **High polycount on background organics.** A 30k-tri rock used 50 times in the background tanks the frame rate. Cap distant organics at 2k.
- **Ignoring MultiMeshInstance3D.** 100 individual MeshInstance3D nodes = 100 draw calls. 100 instances of one MultiMesh = 1 draw call. Same visual result.
- **Adding collision to every leaf and pebble.** Player only needs collision on things the body can hit. Skip it for distant scenery and small ground litter.
- **Using `meshy` (legacy).** No reason to — `trellis` is faster and `hunyuan` is higher quality.

## Edge cases

- **Animated foliage (wind sway).** Generate static here, then add wind sway via a hand-written vertex displacement shader on the material. No animation rig needed.
- **Underwater organics (kelp, anemones).** Same flow; expect Hunyuan to add a "ground attachment" base unless you say `floating, suspended in water`.
- **Branching meshes (vines, roots) come back too thick.** Specify `thin tendril, fine branches`, or accept and scale Y down in the editor.
- **Snow / ice / frozen variant.** Add `covered in snow, frosted, ice crystals` to the prompt — works well on trees and rocks. For temperature variants of the same scene, generate the variant rather than retexturing.
- **Crystal/glass organic.** Mesh comes back opaque. Generate the geometry, then assign a `StandardMaterial3D` with `transparency = ALPHA` and emissive in the editor.
- **Bones, skulls, dead trees.** All work; organic forgives them more than props would. Add `weathered, sun-bleached` for desert / tundra feel.

## Without Summer Engine

In a session without Summer Engine tools (the assets profile; the `summer-assets` skill has the whole loop), do steps 1-4 and skip steps 5-6 (scene wiring, LOD). Save the file where the person asked with `out` (the `summer-assets` skill says how), and tell them the path and format. The file is GLB; level of detail and billboards are the person's engine's job.

## Fallback (no MCP)

1. Run prompts at the Summer dashboard or any 3D-gen web playground (Hunyuan, Trellis, Meshy).
2. Download `.glb` files into `res://assets/organic/`.
3. Build scatter scenes manually in Summer Engine.

For totally free / offline alternatives: **Quaternius** (free stylized organics), **AmbientCG** (rocks + textures), **Sketchfab** free filter, **Polyhaven** (HDRIs + scans).

## Handoff

After the organic models are scattered:

> Forest scatter ready: 3 species at `res://assets/organic/`, 100 instances each via MultiMeshInstance3D in `./World/Forest`. Next:
> - **Wind shader** (sway in breeze): hand-write a vertex displacement shader.
> - **Ground texture** (grass beneath the trees): `asset-strategy` Pipeline 2 for tileable ground.
> - **Lighting / fog** (forest mood): `3d-lighting` for ambient + directional sun + volumetric fog.
> - **Ambient audio** (forest birds, leaves): `ambient-bed`.
> - **Hero props** (a stump, a fallen log, a shrine): `prop-model` for the hand-placed standouts.

## See also

- `prop-model` — for hand-placed standout pieces.
- `environment-kit` — pair with this skill: kit pieces give the architecture, organic gives the natural softness.
- `asset-strategy` — meta-router; ground textures and skyboxes go to Pipeline 2 / panoramic gen.
- `scene-composition` — MultiMeshInstance3D scatter pattern.
- `summer_docs_read` id `reference/mcp-tools-reference` — how to call `assets.generate_3d`; `summer_search` returns its exact input.

skills.description: Build a 2D or 2.5D game as a painted world: a 3D blockout under one fixed camera, an AI paint-over projected onto it, sprite characters.
skills.summary: Build a 2D or 2.5D game as a painted world: a 3D blockout under one fixed camera, an AI paint-over projected onto it, sprite characters.
useWhen: the user asks for a 2D game, a 2.5D game, a top-down RPG, a cozy village or farming game, a dungeon crawler look, or a side-scroller — build the world as a painted 2.5D world, not from a 2D template
the user wants a game that looks like a hand-painted illustration but can be walked around in, with buildings to enter

skills.body:
# Painted 2.5D world

The world looks like one hand-painted illustration, but it is real 3D: the player walks behind houses, enters
buildings and collides with walls. The trick: build the level from cheap blocks, render the blocks from one fixed
camera, have an image model paint over that render, then project the painting back onto the blocks from the same
camera. Characters are 2D sprite sheets standing in the 3D world.

## The rule

**Whenever a user asks for a 2D or 2.5D game** (top-down, RPG, cozy village, adventure, farming, dungeon,
side-scroller, platformer look), build it with this skill. Do not start from a 2D template or a Node2D tile map.
The genre playbooks in `make-game` still decide the mechanics; this skill decides how the world is made and looks.

- Top-down / three-quarter games: camera 30 degrees down, 45 degrees around (houses show two faces). Image
  models draw "isometric" as 2:1 dimetric, which is exactly 30 degrees down; use 30 so the blockout can match a
  generated concept.
- Side-scrollers: the same technique with a camera that looks along the side axis (about 10-20 degrees down,
  0 degrees around) and pans left and right only. Paint one frame per screen-wide chunk.

Tell the user once, before the first character generation or animation: "The world blockout is cheap. Animating
characters costs a couple of dollars in credits and can come out with mistakes; I will check every frame." Then
continue. The blockout, the camera and the projection cost nothing.

## Hard rules (a playtest found each one)

1. **Scale.** Doors 2.5 m. Hero height = door height / 1.15 (2.15 m). One-storey eaves 3.5-4 m, two-storey about
   6 m. Check the hero against a door in the first screenshot.
2. **The gait follows the game type.** Cozy, exploration and RPG games walk by default (about 1.8 m/s, walk cycle)
   and run on Shift (about 4 m/s, run cycle). Action games may run by default (about 4.2 m/s, run cycle). Never
   play the run cycle for the default gait of a cozy game. `painted_player.gd`: `move_speed`, `sprint_speed`,
   `run_cycle_from` (3 m/s).
3. **Animation speed follows ground speed.** A cycle's natural speed is the ground speed at which its feet stick
   (stride per cycle x cycles per second, scaled to the hero height). Each sheet json carries `height_m`,
   `stride_m` and `cycles_per_s` per kind; `speed_scale = speed / natural speed`, clamped. The feet must not
   slide. Never one fixed fps for every speed.
4. **Framing.** The game camera shows about 16 m across (7-8 hero heights). Clamp it inside the painting with
   the real viewport aspect, never an assumed 16:9. The clear colour is the painting's edge colour, per location.
   Rooms are framed whole, like a stage.
5. **At least one enterable building** in every village: a cut-away interior, same view direction, its own 4K
   paint-over, door triggers both ways, a door gap of about 1.8 m. Blockout door and step slabs are hidden in the
   game; the painting shows them.
6. **Eight directions** for idle, walk and run: down, up, left, right, down_left, down_right, up_left, up_right.
   One clip per direction and animation. Mirror only where every frame holds up (never asymmetric hair, a held
   weapon or a walking stick). The player picks the facing by 45 degree sectors.
7. **Blockout proportions from the concept.** Dormers sit on the roof slope (never floating); gables and roofs
   from measured concept pixels; doors 2.5 m; a low block for every flower bed, barrel and crate.
8. **No long cast shadows in the paint.** "Soft short contact shadows only, no long cast shadows on the ground":
   baked long shadows look wrong once the hero walks through them.
9. **Verify in a real window.** Run the game with `-- --shots=<dir>`: `painted_world.gd` walks and runs the hero
   through `shot_plan` (add a walk through each door) and saves a JPG per step. Look at every frame.
10. **Generate a walk whose stride fits the default speed.** Keep the walk cycle's playback within about 1.5x
   (`speed / natural <= 1.5`): a short-step clip played fast looks wrong. Measure the natural walk speed; if it
   is too low, regenerate the walk clips with the brisk long-stride prompt (step 9). The plug-in walks are natural
   at about 1.25-1.4 m/s at 2.15 m, so 1.8 m/s plays at 1.3-1.45x. Short, 4-heads-tall characters reach about
   half a body height per cycle at most; taller proportions (6-7 heads) give longer strides.

## Steps

### 0. The project and the engine

- No project yet: `summer create empty <name>` (or write a plain `project.godot`), open it with
  `summer run <path>`, and check that `summer_get_project_context` answers for that project.
- `engine_not_running` while an editor is open: the editor was started with another HOME, or the MCP is bound to
  a different editor. Start this project's editor with `summer run <path>`, or drive it from a shell with the CLI
  and `SUMMER_ENGINE_PROJECT=<path>` set.
- Image generation through Summer: always pass an `idempotencyKey` and `numImages: 1`. A call that answers
  `outcome_unknown` (a timeout) may still run and charge: retry with the **same** key, never a new one.

### 1. Concept (one image)

`summer_assets_generate_image` with `model: "seedream-5-pro"`, `width` 2048, `height` 1152 (the largest 16:9
image Summer's models return; the others stop near 1024x576):

```
Hand-painted illustration of <place>, rich detail, warm painterly light, seen from a high three-quarter
top-down camera (looking down about 30 degrees, orthographic, no perspective distortion), like a tilted
isometric game map. In the scene: <every object with its rough position: "three cottages around a dirt
plaza, a well with a small roof in the centre, a striped market stall top left, fences, round trees">.
Clean readable shapes, soft brush texture, no characters, no text, no UI, no border.
```

Pick the image the user likes. It is the art direction and the layout.

### 2. Blockout (cheap: you write it)

Write one GDScript or scene that rebuilds the concept **one to one** from the fixed camera: the same building
positions and footprints, roof shapes (gable, hip, dormers on the slope, thatch overhang), chimneys, the well, the
stall, fences, paths, trees and bushes where the concept has them. Use `MeshInstance3D` with `BoxMesh`,
`PrismMesh`, `CylinderMesh`, `SphereMesh` (not CSG: only MeshInstance3D nodes get the painting). Give each
material one flat colour (red = tile roof, yellow =
thatch, dark blue = slate, cream = plaster walls, grey = stone, brown = wood, tall brown slabs = doors, green =
grass, pink low blocks = flower beds): the colours tell the painter what each block is, and the paint-over prompt
repeats them as a colour key. Name door and step slabs `..._door` / `..._steps`: they are hidden in the game.

```
World (Node3D, painted_world.gd: player_path, start_location)
  Village       Node3D, painted_location.gd (paint, frame_whole = false)
    PaintCamera Camera3D  ORTHOGONAL, KEEP_WIDTH, size = frame width in metres (40 for a village square)
                rotation_degrees = Vector3(-30, 45, 0)   # 30 down, 45 around; never change it later
                position = frame centre - forward * 60, far = 200
    Painted     Node3D    every block (or blockout_builder.gd reading a spec), Ground walkable
  Cottage       Node3D, painted_location.gd (frame_whole = true), 100 m off to the side
    PaintCamera same rotation, size 14 for a 9 x 7.5 m room
    Painted     ...
  DoorIn        Area3D, painted_door.gd (to = Cottage, spawn = a Marker3D inside the room)
  DoorOut       Area3D, painted_door.gd (to = Village, spawn = a Marker3D outside the village door)
  GameCamera    Camera3D
  Player        CharacterBody3D, painted_player.gd (sheet, sheet_json)
```

One world script owns the player, the camera and the doors; locations never move the player themselves.
`painted_world.gd` sets the player up after every child is ready, so the node order is free.

In a `.tscn`, the paint camera line for 30 down, 45 around is (Godot writes the basis by rows; hand-written
columns give a wrong camera):
`transform = Transform3D(0.707107, -0.353553, 0.612372, 0, 0.866025, 0.5, -0.707107, -0.353553, 0.612372, cx + 36.742, cy + 30, cz + 36.742)`
for a frame centred on (cx, cy, cz), 60 m back along the view.

**Write the blockout as a spec** (`_building-blocks/blockout_builder.gd` documents the JSON: box, prism, cyl,
sphere, poly ground, invisible wall blockers). The same file drives the engine (the builder is the location's
`Painted` node) and an engine-free wireframe preview over the concept (`tools/preview.py`), so the fitting loop
needs no engine runs.

- **Gable roofs are two parts:** a wall-coloured prism for the gable triangle plus two thin slanted roof slabs
  with an overhang. A single roof-coloured prism makes the painter paint roof on the gable wall.
- **Edges and water:** put invisible `wall` blockers along water and ledge edges, with gaps at pier roots and
  doorways. Ground made from a polygon is one-sided: use the spec's `poly` (two-sided collision) or a box.

Solid things get a `StaticBody3D` and a box/cylinder shape: walls, trunks, fence posts, the well, furniture.
Things the player walks behind need real height (houses, trees, stalls).

**Paint richness follows blockout density.** The painter details what the blocks give it. Add low blocks for
flower beds, barrels, crates, benches, lanterns and window boxes wherever the concept has them; a sparse blockout
comes back as a sparse painting. Only truly flat detail (cobbles, rugs, grass) can stay paint-only.

**Match the concept.** Read positions straight from the concept by inverting the orthographic camera
(`tools/cam.py <height> <px,py> ...` does it). With the
concept W x H pixels, `s` = pixels per metre (W / frame width), `elev` = 30 degrees and a pixel (sx, sy) on the
ground (a wall's bottom corner):

```
u = (sx - W/2) / s                      # metres along the camera's right axis
v = (H/2 - sy) / (s * sin(elev))        # metres along the ground, away from the camera
height = dy / (s * cos(elev))           # a vertical edge dy pixels long (wall, ridge, chimney)
world = target + right_ground * u + far_ground * v
```

Three wall-bottom corners give a footprint; the ridge gives the roof height. Draw the spec over the concept with
`tools/preview.py` and move blocks until the red silhouettes line up, then build it in the engine.
If the blockout does not match the concept, the painting will not match the blocks.

### 3. Render the blockout from the paint camera

- Play with the location's `paint` left empty: `painted_world.gd` then shows the blockout through that
  `PaintCamera`, lit by a sun and ambient light so its faces read (an unlit blockout comes out near black).
  `summer_screenshot` `target: "game"` captures it.
- Exact PNG for the painter: copy `_building-blocks/capture_paint_view.gd`, make a scene with just that node
  (`level` = the world scene, `camera_path` = the location's camera, `size` = 2048x1152), and play it in a run
  that renders (the editor, or a windowed run; `--headless` renders nothing). It saves
  `res://painted/blockout.png` and quits.
- `summer_screenshot` `target: "scene"` renders the saved scene without running scripts: a blockout built by a
  script or the spec builder shows nothing there.

Then upload it: `summer_call` `assets.upload_begin`, post its form fields plus the file to `uploadUrl`, then
`assets.upload_complete` with `publicId`, `version`, `uploadSignature` (the `signature` of the upload's answer)
and `format`. Its answer carries the `fileUrl`.

### 4. Paint-over (strict image to image)

**Never pass the whole concept as a reference.** Even when the blockout rebuilds it one to one, frontier edit
models copy the full concept and ignore the blocks. Pass a **material sheet** instead: a 2x2 grid of close-up
crops from the concept (for a village: clay-tile roof with a timber-framed wall, thatch, market stall with
cobbles, slate roof with flower beds). It carries the style and materials but no layout.

With two images (image 1 = blockout render, image 2 = material sheet), the best frontier edit model you have, 16:9,
the largest size (4K):

```
Image 1 is a flat-coloured 3D blockout render of <place> from a fixed game camera. Image 2 is a sheet of four
close-up material samples from the finished concept art (<the four samples>). Image 2 is a style and
material reference only: never copy its layout or composition.
Repaint image 1 in exactly that style, materials, light and detail. This is a strict image-to-image
paint-over: keep every shape, edge and position of image 1 identical, pixel-aligned. Same camera, same
framing. Every <building, roof, chimney, dormer, door, steps, well, stall, crate, bench, barrel, fence, tree and
bush> stays exactly where image 1 has it, with exactly the same silhouette and size. Do not add, remove or move
anything. Do not add extra props, buildings or trees. Only paint surface detail inside the existing shapes.
Colour key of image 1: red = clay-tile roof, yellow = golden thatch roof, dark blue = slate roof, cream =
timber-framed plaster walls, grey = mossy stone (chimneys, well, low walls, steps), brown = worn wood (tall
brown slabs on walls = wooden doors), light brown floor = cobblestone plaza, green ground = grass, green
spheres = round leafy tree canopies, small green domes = flowering bushes, orange = lit lanterns and fruit
crates, pink low blocks = dense flower beds and window boxes.
<Light and finish: e.g. warm golden late-afternoon light, soft short contact shadows only (no long cast shadows
on the ground), glowing windows, painterly near-realistic detail as in image 2: ivy on walls, moss on stones,
rich textures>. No characters, no text, no border.
```

`summer_assets_generate_image` takes one `referenceImageUrl` (the blockout render): put the material and
style description into the prompt in words and keep the colour key. Use `model: "seedream-5-pro"`, `width`
2048, `height` 1152, `numImages: 1` and an `idempotencyKey`: it holds pixel alignment well and is the only
Summer model that returns 2048 px.

**Check alignment before you use it.** Overlay the blockout's edges (red) on the painting
(`tools/overlay.py <blockout.png> <painting.png> <out.png>`) and look: roof lines,
wall corners, the well and the stall must sit on the red lines. Reject any painting where objects moved, were
added, or the framing zoomed; generate again rather than project a drifted painting.

### 5. Resolution

Painting pixels per metre must be at least the screen's pixels per metre. A 4K painting (about 5500 px) over a
40 m frame gives 137 px/m; a 16 m view on a 1080p-class game view needs about 96-120 px/m, so it stays sharp. A
2048 px painting over 32 m (64 px/m) is soft at that view. For bigger worlds use more frames, not a wider frame.

**4K through Summer:** no Summer image model returns 4K. `tools/detail4k.py <painting_2k.png> <out_dir> "<style
words>"` upscales the 2K paint-over 2x, cuts nine overlapping 2048x1152 tiles, runs a strict "redraw sharper,
pixel-aligned" image-to-image pass on each with `seedream-5-pro` and blends them back. Nine generations; the
alignment holds.

### 6. Projection in the engine

Copy `_building-blocks/paint_projection.gdshader`, `painted_location.gd`, `painted_world.gd`,
`painted_door.gd` and `painted_player.gd` to `res://painted/`. Set each location's `paint`. On `_ready` a
location puts one `ShaderMaterial` on every mesh under its `Painted`; the shader takes each surface point's
position in that location's paint camera frame as its UV. No UV unwrapping, no baking.

- Keep the scene's tonemap **Linear**, exposure 1, no glow, no fog: the painting already holds the light.
- Import the painting lossless (Import dock: Compress Mode Lossless, mipmaps on); VRAM compression smears it.
- Verify: `_building-blocks/paintcam_check.gd` renders the painted world through a `PaintCamera` to a PNG; it
  must match the painting. Then play and look at the real window (hard rule 9).

### 7. Camera rules

- The game camera has the paint camera's direction and only **moves** (follows the player). With an orthographic
  camera, moving never reveals a surface the painting did not see. Never orbit or tilt it: turned views show the
  painting's mistakes (a painted chimney next to the real one, roof edges smeared on the ground).
- Outdoors it shows about 16 m across; rooms are framed whole. `painted_world.gd` sizes and clamps it with the
  real viewport aspect and sets the clear colour to the painting's edge colour.
- More world = more frames. Every frame uses the same direction, its own paint camera position and painting.
  Paint neighbouring frames with an overlap strip so the seams match.

### 8. Interiors

Every village gets at least one enterable building. Each interior is its own location far away (for example 100 m
off to the side) with the **same** camera direction and a frame that holds the whole room with its back walls
(14 m for a 9 x 7.5 m room; 12 m cut the walls off), `frame_whole = true`. Lower
the two walls nearest the camera to knee height (a dollhouse cut-away) and leave a door gap of about 1.8 m.
Blockout, render, paint over (its own 4K paint-over, the same rules and colour key: warm floorboards, plaster,
beams, fireplace, bed, shelves, rug, "keep the area outside the room plain flat dark") and project exactly like
the outside. `painted_door.gd` triggers go both ways; put each spawn marker clear of the other door's trigger.

### 9. Characters

1. **Ready-made:** use the painted plug-in characters first: a man, a woman, the man with a sword and an old man,
   8 directions, idle, walk and run (`hero_m_sword`: idle and walk). They live in the public repo
   `SummerEngine/painted-characters`, pinned at commit `c70dae1b4043656ad23d5ab6d76fe992f593b6ba`. For `<id>`, import
   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SummerEngine/painted-characters/c70dae1b4043656ad23d5ab6d76fe992f593b6ba/characters/<id>/<file>`
   for the three files `<id>_sheet.png`, `<id>_sheet.json` and `<id>_frames.tres` into `res://characters/<id>/`
   (`summer_import_from_url`; the `.tres` expects that path), then set `sheet` = `<id>_sheet.png` and
   `sheet_json` = `<id>_sheet.json` on `painted_player.gd`. With a shell, `git clone` the repo and copy
   `characters/` to the project root. Need a different look: make one.
2. **New character:** generate an 8-pose turnaround (or two 4-pose sheets) in the world's style on flat pure
   green:
   ```
   Character turnaround sheet in the art style of <the world>: <character>. Draw the same character 8 times,
   same size, feet on one baseline: facing down toward the viewer, down-left, left, up-left, up (back view),
   up-right, right, down-right. Seen from a high three-quarter top-down camera. Plain flat pure green
   background (#00FF00), no ground, no shadows, no text.
   ```
   Crop each pose, pad it to 9:16 with the same green, upload it, then `summer_call` `assets.generate_video`
   (`model: "minimax-h3-max"`, `aspectRatio: "9:16"`, 5 s, an `idempotencyKey`): one clip per direction and
   animation:
   ```
   The character, <facing>, walks in place on the spot with a brisk, purposeful walk cycle: long confident strides, heel to toe, the front leg reaching far forward and the back leg pushing far back, arms swinging strongly opposite the legs, upright posture. The character
   stays exactly centred at the same size and never moves across the frame or turns. Static locked camera, no
   zoom. The plain flat pure green background stays perfectly flat and unchanged. Seamless loop.
   ```
   That is the walk prompt for a default walk (a plain "steady, simple walk cycle" takes short steps and must be
   over-sped). For a longer stride still: "walks in place on the spot with a long-legged power walk: very wide
   steps, at each step the front heel lands far ahead and the back foot pushes off far behind, legs nearly fully
   extended front to back, arms swinging wide, a quick purposeful pace."
   Idle: "stands still in a relaxed idle: gentle breathing, one blink, feet planted". Run: "runs in place".
3. **Clip to sheet** (host with a shell and ffmpeg): key out the green by colour, take one cycle (skip the
   first second), sample 8 frames evenly, crop every frame of every clip with the **same** box so the feet stay
   on one line, and tile them into one sheet: one row per animation and direction (`idle_down`,
   `walk_up_left`, `run_right`, ...). Write the json beside it: `{"cell_w", "cell_h", "frames", "rows",
   "fps": {"idle", "walk", "run"}, "height_m", "stride_m": {"walk", "run"}, "cycles_per_s": {"walk", "run"}}`.
   Measure once per kind: `stride_m` = how far a planted foot slides back during one cycle at `height_m`,
   `cycles_per_s` = cycles per second at the sheet's fps. Look at every frame; regenerate a clip with a broken
   frame.
   Without video: `summer_call` `assets.generate_sprite_sheet` (8-frame walk from one picture, per direction).
4. **In the game:** `painted_player.gd` makes an `AnimatedSprite3D`: Y-billboard, unshaded, alpha cut (so painted
   walls hide the character), height stretched by `1 / cos(camera pitch)`, 8 facings by 45 degree sectors (a
   missing diagonal falls back to its side row), the game-type gait (hard rule 2), animation speed = speed /
   natural speed.
   Spawn points 0.5 m or more away from walls, or the flat card cuts into them.

### 10. Weapons

- **Variant sheet (best look):** edit the turnaround so the character holds the weapon, then animate the clips
  again. One extra sheet per weapon. Never mirror a sheet with a held weapon.
- **Held sprite layer (cheap):** a second `Sprite3D` child with the weapon, a per-direction offset and draw order
  (behind the body when facing up). Good for many weapons; the hand will not wrap around the grip.

## Common mistakes

- **The whole concept as a reference:** the painting copies the concept and ignores the blocks, even when the
  blockout matches it. Pass a 2x2 material sheet cropped from the concept.
- **A sparse blockout:** the painting comes back sparse. Add low blocks for flower beds, crates, barrels, benches.
- **35 degrees against a generated concept:** generated "isometric" art is 30 degrees down; the blocks will not fit.
- **A tiny or giant hero:** check the hero against a door (door = hero x 1.15) in the first screenshot.
- **Sliding feet or the wrong gait:** speed_scale = speed / natural; cozy games walk by default and run on Shift.
- **4096 px asked from Summer's image models:** refused. 2048x1152 with seedream-5-pro, then the tiled 4K pass.
- **A new idempotencyKey after a timeout:** pays twice. Retry with the same key; keep numImages 1.
- **An unlit blockout capture, CSG blocks, a one-sided polygon ground, no water blockers:** see steps 2 and 3.
- **Long baked shadows:** they lie on the ground while the hero walks through them. Contact shadows only.
- **Floating dormers, blockout door slabs left visible:** dormers on the slope; hide door and step slabs.
- **Rotating the game camera:** shows painted detail on the wrong surfaces. Translate only.
- **Filmic/ACES tonemap or lights on painted meshes:** colours shift. Unshaded material, Linear tonemap.
- **Perspective camera:** moving it reveals hidden faces. Use orthographic.
- **Assuming a 16:9 window:** the clamp shows past the painting in the editor's game view. Use the real aspect.

## Optional: Blender route

If the host has Blender, `_building-blocks/blender-route.md` bakes the same projection into ordinary UVs and
exports glTF; use it when the scene must ship as plain textured meshes.

## See also

- `make-game` (genre mechanics), `concept-art`, `sprite-sheet`, `scene-composition`
